turbo-driven-by-exhaust.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

differential-why.fact: In a turn the outer wheels travel farther than the inner ones, so they must turn faster. A differential lets the two wheels on a driven axle rotate at different speeds; vehicles without one, like go-karts, rely on the tyres slipping in corners.
differential-why.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

diesel-no-spark-plugs.fact: A diesel engine has no spark plugs: it compresses air until it is hot enough to ignite the fuel as it is injected (compression ignition). Some diesels, especially indirect-injection types, are harder to start and need glow plugs.
diesel-no-spark-plugs.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

dpf-needs-a-drive.fact: A diesel particulate filter traps soot and must burn it off from time to time (regeneration). This needs higher road speeds than city streets usually allow, so a diesel driven only in town traffic may need regular faster drives; ignoring the warning light too long can ruin the filter so it must be replaced.
dpf-needs-a-drive.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

immobiliser-chip-key.fact: An immobiliser lets the engine start only when it recognises the electronic chip (transponder) in the correct key. Immobilisers have been mandatory on all new cars in Germany since 1 January 1998 and in the UK since 1 October 1998.
immobiliser-chip-key.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

speedometer-reads-high.fact: Under UN regulation ECE R39 a speedometer may never show less than the true speed, and may show at most 10% plus 4 km/h more at the test speeds. Tyre size affects the reading too: most speedometers have tolerances of about plus or minus 10%, mainly because of differences in tyre diameter.
speedometer-reads-high.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

fuel-filler-arrow.fact: On many dashboards a small arrow next to the fuel-pump icon points to the side of the car where the fuel filler is. The icon-and-arrow idea came from Ford designer Jim Moylan in 1986.
fuel-filler-arrow.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

headlamp-lens-cloudy.fact: Plastic (polycarbonate) headlamp lenses turn cloudy and yellow because ultraviolet light from the sun and the bulbs oxidises the lens hardcoat. Mild haze can be polished out, but sanding without a new UV-resistant clear coat makes the lens degrade faster. Aim matters too: misaimed headlamps are dangerous and ineffective.
headlamp-lens-cloudy.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

snow-chains-slow.fact: Snow chains go on the driven wheels and are for slow driving: chain manuals generally set a maximum of about 30 to 50 km/h.
snow-chains-slow.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

esc-mandatory-dates.fact: Electronic stability control brakes individual wheels to keep the car going where the steering points. It became mandatory on new passenger cars in the US from model year 2012 and on all newly registered cars in the EU from 1 November 2014; in Europe it had saved an estimated 15,000 lives by 2020.
esc-mandatory-dates.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

airbag-milliseconds.fact: In a frontal crash the decision to fire the airbags is typically made within 15 to 30 milliseconds, and the front airbags are fully inflated within about 60 to 80 milliseconds. Airbags are a supplemental restraint system (SRS), designed to work with the seat belt, not to replace it.
airbag-milliseconds.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

rear-facing-seat-airbag.fact: A rear-facing infant seat in a front seat with an active airbag puts the baby's head close to the airbag, and its deployment can cause severe head injuries or death. Some cars have a switch to disable the front passenger airbag.
rear-facing-seat-airbag.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

hot-car-window-myth.fact: At 21 °C outside, a car standing in direct sun can pass 49 °C inside within a short time; children and older people can suffer heat stroke in minutes, and a window left slightly open does not prevent it.
hot-car-window-myth.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

who-seatbelt-child-restraint.fact: WHO: wearing a seat belt cuts the risk of death for people in a vehicle by as much as 50%, and using child restraints can cut deaths of infants by 71%.
who-seatbelt-child-restraint.licence_note: World Health Organization fact sheet (copyright WHO). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

who-speed-risk.fact: WHO: each 1% rise in average speed raises the risk of a fatal crash by 4% and the risk of a serious crash by 3%. For a pedestrian struck by the front of a car, the risk of dying is 4.5 times higher at 65 km/h than at 50 km/h.
who-speed-risk.licence_note: World Health Organization fact sheet (copyright WHO). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

who-phone-hands-free.fact: WHO: a driver on a mobile phone is roughly 4 times as likely to crash; hands-free use is not much safer than holding the phone, and texting raises the risk a lot.
who-phone-hands-free.licence_note: World Health Organization fact sheet (copyright WHO). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

who-road-deaths-young.fact: WHO: road crashes kill about 1.16 million people a year, and for people aged 5 to 29 (children and young adults) road injuries are the top cause of death.
who-road-deaths-young.licence_note: World Health Organization fact sheet (copyright WHO). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

benz-patent-1886.fact: Carl Benz filed his patent application for a motor carriage on 29 January 1886; the patent, DRP 37435, gave the Benz Patent-Motorwagen its name.
benz-patent-1886.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

bertha-benz-first-trip.fact: On 5 August 1888 Bertha Benz made the first long-distance drive in a petrol car, about 106 km from Mannheim to Pforzheim in the Patent-Motorwagen. Its fuel, a solvent called ligroin, was sold only by pharmacies, so the pharmacy in Wiesloch became the world's first filling station.
bertha-benz-first-trip.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

bertha-benz-brake-lining.fact: On that same 1888 trip Bertha Benz used her hat pin to clear a blocked fuel line, and when the wooden brakes started to give out she had a shoemaker cover them with leather: the first brake linings.
bertha-benz-brake-lining.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

model-t-assembly-line.fact: Ford's moving assembly line started on 7 October 1913 and cut the time to build a Model T from about 12.5 hours to 93 minutes by 1914. More than 15 million Model Ts were sold.
model-t-assembly-line.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

model-t-any-colour-black.fact: Henry Ford later wrote that in 1909 he told his managers customers could have a car in any colour as long as it was black; the black-only policy was actually put into practice only in 1914.
model-t-any-colour-black.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

wiper-mary-anderson.fact: Mary Anderson was granted a patent for a hand-operated windshield wiper in 1903. Potential buyers saw no commercial value in it, and her 17-year patent expired in 1920 without the device going into mass production.
wiper-mary-anderson.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

electric-starter-1912.fact: Before the electric starter, cars were started with a hand crank. Charles Kettering's electrical system for starting, ignition and lighting went into Cadillac's 1912 models, for which Cadillac ordered 12,000 self-starters.
electric-starter-1912.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

first-traffic-light-1868.fact: In December 1868, before any car existed, the first traffic signals went up outside London's Houses of Parliament, so that fewer police officers were needed to direct traffic. A policeman moved semaphore arms by day and worked red and green lamps at night; on 2 January 1869 the signal exploded and was removed.
first-traffic-light-1868.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

three-point-belt-free-patent.fact: The modern three-point seat belt was developed by Nils Bohlin for Volvo, which introduced it as standard in 1959, and Volvo then made the patent open so other car makers could use the design for free. Bohlin showed its effect in a study of 28,000 crashes in Sweden.
three-point-belt-free-patent.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

abs-first-1978.fact: One of the first electronic four-wheel anti-lock braking systems, made by Bosch, was offered as an option on the Mercedes-Benz S-Class (W116) from 1978.
abs-first-1978.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

first-speeding-fine-1896.fact: Walter Arnold of East Peckham in Kent is thought to be the first driver ever convicted of speeding: on 28 January 1896 he went at 8 mph (13 km/h) and was fined 1 shilling plus costs. Under the 1865 Red Flag Act the town limit was 2 mph (3 km/h).
first-speeding-fine-1896.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

cruise-control-blind-inventor.fact: Cruise control was invented by Ralph Teetor, who was blind. Family lore says that riding with his lawyer, who slowed down while talking and sped up while listening, annoyed him into inventing a speed control; his 'Speedostat' was patented in 1950, and Cadillac marketed it as 'Cruise Control'.
cruise-control-blind-inventor.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

rear-view-mirror-1911.fact: The earliest known rear-view mirror on a racing car was on Ray Harroun's Marmon at the first Indianapolis 500 in 1911; Harroun said the rough brick track shook it so much that it was of little use. Mirrors for cars had already been written about in 1906, and an adjustable dashboard mirror was sold in 1908.
rear-view-mirror-1911.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

crumple-zone-patent.fact: Mercedes-Benz patent No. 854157, granted in 1952 to engineer Béla Barényi's design, divided the car body into a rigid passenger compartment and front and rear crumple zones that absorb crash energy, against the old belief that a safe car had to be rigid. The first Mercedes body built with it was the 1959 W111.
crumple-zone-patent.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

leaded-petrol-end-2021.fact: Leaded petrol for cars was phased out worldwide only in July 2021, when Algeria stopped selling it; the UN Environment Programme declared its official end on 30 August 2021. Lead poisons catalytic converters, so cars with one can run only on unleaded fuel.
leaded-petrol-end-2021.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

prius-first-hybrid.fact: The Toyota Prius was the first mass-produced hybrid car: it went on sale in Japan in 1997 and worldwide in 2000.
prius-first-hybrid.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

corolla-best-seller.fact: The Toyota Corolla has been the best-selling car nameplate of all time since 1997, when it passed the Volkswagen Beetle; Toyota reached 50 million Corollas sold in 2021.
corolla-best-seller.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

beetle-last-one-2003.fact: The original Volkswagen Beetle was built from 1938 to 2003; the last one left the Puebla plant in Mexico on 30 July 2003, after 21,529,464 had been made, the most of any car on a single platform.
beetle-last-one-2003.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

jdm-180-limit.fact: Most cars built for Japan's home market are limited to 180 km/h. The limit is self-imposed by the makers through the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association and is not a legal requirement.
jdm-180-limit.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

kei-car-rules.fact: Japan's kei cars are limited by law to 3.4 m long, 1.48 m wide, under 2.0 m high and an engine under 660 cc; a gentlemen's agreement among makers also caps power at 64 PS.
kei-car-rules.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

japan-shaken-inspection.fact: Under Japan's shaken programme a private car needs its first inspection after three years and then one every two years.
japan-shaken-inspection.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

fuel-saving-gadgets-myth.fact: The US EPA tested over 100 supposed fuel-saving devices, such as fuel-line magnets and mixture 'enhancers'; very few gave any benefit, and some could damage the engine or increase exhaust emissions.
fuel-saving-gadgets-myth.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

phone-at-pump-myth.fact: The story that a mobile phone can ignite petrol at a pump has not been reproduced under any controlled conditions; phone makers and stations still ask people to switch phones off. The documented refuelling fires involve static electricity: a driver who does not first touch a conductive part of the car carries the charge to the nozzle, and many stations warn against leaving the pump while refuelling.
phone-at-pump-myth.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

petrol-in-diesel-damage.fact: Petrol in a diesel is the costly mix-up: in a modern diesel even one litre of petrol can wreck the injection pump for good, because petrol does not lubricate it. Diesel put in a petrol engine makes heavy smoke but, drained as soon as it is noticed, usually leaves no lasting damage.
petrol-in-diesel-damage.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

aggressive-driving-fuel.fact: Aggressive driving (speeding, rapid acceleration and hard braking) can lower fuel economy by roughly 15% to 30% at highway speeds and 10% to 40% in stop-and-go traffic.
aggressive-driving-fuel.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

speed-above-80-fuel.fact: Every car has its own most efficient speed, but fuel economy usually drops rapidly above about 80 km/h (50 mph).
speed-above-80-fuel.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

extra-weight-fuel.fact: An extra 100 pounds (about 45 kg) in the car can reduce fuel economy by about 1%; the effect is larger on smaller cars.
extra-weight-fuel.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

roof-box-fuel.fact: A large, blunt roof-top cargo box can reduce fuel economy by around 2% to 8% in city driving, 6% to 17% on the highway and 10% to 25% at 105 to 120 km/h (65 to 75 mph).
roof-box-fuel.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

cruise-control-saves-fuel.fact: On the highway, cruise control helps hold a constant speed and in most cases saves fuel.
cruise-control-saves-fuel.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

odometer-rollback-scale.fact: A 2002 NHTSA study estimated that 450,000 vehicles a year were sold in the US with false odometer readings, costing buyers over $1 billion a year. Digital odometers can be even easier to tamper with, often through the OBD2 port; wear on floor mats and pedal rubber that does not fit the mileage is a warning sign.
odometer-rollback-scale.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

salvage-title-meaning.fact: In the US a 'salvage' title brand goes on a car that an insurer paid out on as damaged or a total loss; how much damage that takes depends on the state, from 50% to 95% of the car's value. 'Salvage', 'rebuilt' and similar brands differ from state to state, and a car exported from the US can get a clean title whatever its history.
salvage-title-meaning.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

title-washing.fact: 'Title washing' means re-registering a car in another jurisdiction for the purpose of removing a brand such as 'salvage' from its title; vehicle history reports are meant to reveal it.
title-washing.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

recall-check-by-vin.fact: Any US car's 17-character VIN can be checked free on NHTSA's recall site for unrepaired safety recalls; the search does not show recalls more than 15 years old, unless a maker offers longer coverage.
recall-check-by-vin.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). nhtsa.gov blocks automated fetching, so the fact was checked through the site's own indexed page text; restated in our own words.

takata-airbag-recall.fact: The Takata airbag recall is the largest car recall in US history, covering more than 42 million US cars; by January 2024 over 100 million inflators had been recalled worldwide by more than 20 car makers. A faulty inflator can rupture and throw metal fragments, and Takata said the issue was linked to hot, humid locations.
takata-airbag-recall.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

us-used-cars-to-georgia.fact: Georgia is one of the main destinations for used American-made vehicles: an October 2020 report put the United Arab Emirates first, followed by Nigeria and Georgia.
us-used-cars-to-georgia.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

miles-to-km.fact: American odometers count miles: one international mile is exactly 1.609344 km, so 100,000 miles is about 160,934 km.
miles-to-km.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

georgia-car-trade-2025.fact: Geostat data for 2025: motor cars were Georgia's top export, USD 2.8 billion or 38.6% of all exports, and motor vehicles were also the top import, USD 3.8 billion or 20.9% of imports.
georgia-car-trade-2025.licence_note: News report (facts only, restated in our own words, no text copied). Secondary source: prefer the official act if the figure is ever disputed.

ge-inspection-schedule.fact: Georgia's periodic technical inspection started on 1 January 2018 and has been mandatory for every vehicle category since 1 January 2019. A passenger car (category M1) is inspected every second year once it is 4 years old, and every year once it is 8 years old.
ge-inspection-schedule.licence_note: Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development of Georgia, official page. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words.

ge-inspection-checklist.fact: Georgia's periodic inspection checks the vehicle's identification, braking system, steering, visibility, lamps, reflectors and electrics, axles, wheels, tyres and suspension, the chassis, and environmental nuisance such as exhaust emissions.
ge-inspection-checklist.licence_note: Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development of Georgia, official page. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words.

ge-steering-conversion-fails.fact: Georgia (the economy ministry's inspection page, rules from 2018, under right-hand-drive vehicles): a right-hand-drive car first registered in Georgia after 1 January 2018 cannot pass the periodic inspection if its steering system has been further changed, and once an inspection from that date has recorded the steering wheel's side, moving the wheel again also means the car cannot pass.
ge-steering-conversion-fails.licence_note: Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development of Georgia, official page. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words.

ge-gas-sticker.fact: Georgia (Government Resolution No. 80 of 15 January 2014, for equipment that runs a car on natural gas, i.e. methane/CNG): this gas-cylinder equipment gets its own compliance check, and a car that passes gets a round blue sticker 90 mm across in the lower right corner of the windshield, with its expiry month in red figures. The resolution's forms call it a mandatory yearly assessment.
ge-gas-sticker.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-gas-no-fill-overdue.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 80, natural gas / CNG): a driver must not fill gas cylinders that have not passed their next periodic check and lack the matching stamp, and must not fill them if a leak has been found in the gas lines or joints.
ge-gas-no-fill-overdue.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-gas-smell-stop.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 80, natural gas / CNG): if the driver smells gas while driving, they must stop at once, fix the fault if they can or close the supply valve, and go to a gas-equipment service.
ge-gas-smell-stop.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-gas-extinguisher-no-flame.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 80, natural gas / CNG): every vehicle with natural-gas cylinders must carry a fire extinguisher and a felt fire blanket, and in cold weather the engine and frozen gas lines may be warmed only with hot water, hot air or steam, never an open flame.
ge-gas-extinguisher-no-flame.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-gas-cylinder-rejected.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 80, natural gas / CNG): a cylinder is refused at the check if it lacks the required markings (maker's mark, number, dates of manufacture and periodic check, working and test pressure, mass) or some of them cannot be read, or if it has cracks, damaged threads, or gouges and scratches deeper than 10% of the wall thickness.
ge-gas-cylinder-rejected.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-gas-filling-order.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 80): at the station, natural gas cylinders are filled with the engine off and the outlet valve closed, up to the working pressure of 20 MPa (200 atm); afterwards the outlet valve is opened gradually, and only then is the engine started.
ge-gas-filling-order.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-speed-limits.fact: Georgian traffic law for category B cars: up to 60 km/h in built-up areas and 20 km/h in residential zones; elsewhere up to 110 km/h on motorways and 90 km/h on other roads, or 80 km/h on any road when towing a light trailer. Road signs can set different limits.
ge-speed-limits.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-children-front-seat.fact: Georgian traffic law: children under 12 may not ride in a car's front seat. A child under 3 in the back must sit in a child seat or restraint that fits their height and weight, or on the lap of a back-seat passenger aged at least 16 who wears a seat belt, with no more than one child per lap.
ge-children-front-seat.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-seatbelt-who-must.fact: Georgian traffic law: the driver must wear a seat belt and make sure the passenger beside them wears one, as must a rear passenger aged 16 or over who holds a child under 3 on their lap.
ge-seatbelt-who-must.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-phone-ban.fact: Georgian traffic law: drivers may not use a mobile phone while driving, except through a headset or a loudspeaker (remote) talk function while both hands stay free for driving.
ge-phone-ban.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-dazzled-stop-hazards.fact: Georgian traffic law: if oncoming headlights dazzle you, slow down without changing lanes, stop and switch on the hazard lights; drive on only once your sight has fully recovered.
ge-dazzled-stop-hazards.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-tunnel-rules.fact: Georgian traffic law: in a tunnel marked by a road sign, the headlights (dipped or main beam) must be on even if the tunnel is lit; reversing and U-turns are banned, and stopping is allowed only in an emergency, in a marked bay if there is one.
ge-tunnel-rules.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-fog-lamp-colours.fact: Georgian traffic law: front fog lamps, if fitted, must give white or selective yellow light, two on a car, and no part of their lit surface may be above the top of the dipped headlamps; rear fog lamps must be red.
ge-fog-lamp-colours.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-winter-tyre-period.fact: Georgia (Government Resolution No. 526, in force since 1 January 2024): from 1 December to 1 March, every wheel must have proper winter tyres on the road sections the resolution lists; in extreme weather the Interior Minister can set a different period.
ge-winter-tyre-period.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-winter-tyre-spec.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 526): a tyre counts as a winter tyre only if less than 10 years have passed since its manufacture date, the date is readable, the tread is at least 3 mm deep on cars (4 mm on buses) and it carries the snowflake symbol.
ge-winter-tyre-spec.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-winter-roads-list.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 526) lists the winter-tyre road sections, among them Mleta to Kobi on the Gudauri road, the Rikoti tunnel to Tseva, Borjomi to Bakuriani and Akhalkalaki, Jvari to Mestia and Lasdili, and Tbilisi to Tianeti.
ge-winter-roads-list.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-winter-chains-police.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 526): in extreme weather the police can also require anti-skid chains on all wheels of at least one driven axle; chains must be factory-made, fit the tyre size and be used only on snow or ice, and a driver without proper tyres or chains can be refused entry to the section.
ge-winter-chains-police.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-jvari-pass-bypass.fact: The Jvari Pass, at 2,379 m, is the highest point of the road from Tbilisi to the Russian border; in about 25 km the road climbs more than 1,000 m to reach it. Because the pass is prone to heavy snowfall, a 23 km bypass from Kvesheti to Kobi with a 9 km tunnel, the longest in the region, has been under construction since 2021.
ge-jvari-pass-bypass.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

ge-rikoti-tunnel.fact: The Rikoti Pass (996 m) divides Georgia into its western and eastern parts; the Tbilisi to Kutaisi highway passes through it in a 1,722 m rock-cut tunnel built in 1982.
ge-rikoti-tunnel.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

ge-number-plates.fact: Georgia's current number plates, two letters, three digits and two letters (AA-123-AA), have been issued since 1 September 2014, with the flag and 'GE' on a blue strip; the country code changed from GEO to GE in 2010.
ge-number-plates.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

ge-old-plate-regions.fact: On Georgian plates of the 1993 to 2014 format, the first letter originally showed where the car was registered: A Tbilisi, B Adjara, D Kutaisi, E Rustavi, O Gori, R Telavi and so on, until the system ran out in 2004.
ge-old-plate-regions.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

hc-break-every-two-hours.fact: UK Highway Code rule 91: driving tired greatly raises the risk of a collision; a break of at least 15 minutes after every two hours of driving is recommended, long journeys between midnight and 6 am (when natural alertness is lowest) are best avoided, and if you feel sleepy, stop in a safe place.
hc-break-every-two-hours.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-before-setting-off.fact: UK Highway Code rule 97: before setting off, the mirrors and the seat should be adjusted for comfort, full control and maximum vision, and the head restraint adjusted to reduce the risk of neck and spine injuries in a collision.
hc-before-setting-off.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-mirrors-blind-spots.fact: UK Highway Code rules 159 and 161: mirrors do not cover every area and there are blind spots; before moving off, use all mirrors, look round to check the blind spots, and look round once more before you go.
hc-mirrors-blind-spots.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-reversing-checks.fact: UK Highway Code rules 201 to 203: never reverse from a side road into a main road, and no further than necessary; before reversing look carefully all round, then reverse slowly, looking mainly through the rear window, aware that the front of the car swings out as you turn.
hc-reversing-checks.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-door-far-hand.fact: UK Highway Code rule 239: you must not hit anyone when you open your door; open it with the hand on the opposite side to the door (for example the left hand for a door on your right), which makes you turn your head and look over your shoulder for cyclists and other traffic.
hc-door-far-hand.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-sun-dazzle.fact: UK Highway Code rule 237: if you are dazzled by bright sunlight, slow down and, if necessary, stop.
hc-sun-dazzle.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-limit-not-target.fact: UK Highway Code rule 125: the speed limit is the absolute maximum and does not mean it is safe to drive at that speed whatever the conditions.
hc-limit-not-target.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

ge-uphill-priority.fact: Georgian traffic law (Article 35): on mountain roads and similar steep roads, and on roads marked with signs 1.14 and 1.15, where passing an oncoming vehicle is impossible or difficult, the driver going downhill must stop and give way to the driver going uphill, unless there is a passing place in front of the uphill driver where they can stop. If one of the two must reverse, a vehicle combination has priority over all others, a heavy vehicle over a light one, a bus over trucks and cars; between vehicles of the same category the downhill one reverses, unless it is clearly easier for the uphill one (for example, it is near a passing place).
ge-uphill-priority.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald), consolidated version of 25/06/2026. Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-left-lane-rule.fact: Georgian traffic law (Article 31): outside built-up areas, and in towns on stretches where more than 80 km/h is allowed, drivers must keep as close to the right edge as possible; occupying the left lane while the right lane is free is forbidden, except to go round an obstacle, turn left or make a U-turn (overtaking is done on the left, Article 34). With three or more lanes in one direction, the far-left lane may be used only in heavy traffic when the other lanes are full, or to overtake, turn left or U-turn (trucks only to turn left or U-turn).
ge-left-lane-rule.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald), consolidated version of 25/06/2026. Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-signals-give-no-priority.fact: Georgian traffic law (Article 48): sounding the horn or flashing the headlights gives a driver no priority over other road users. In towns, an intention to overtake may be signalled with the lights (short on-off flashes by day, switching dipped to main beam at night).
ge-signals-give-no-priority.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald), consolidated version of 25/06/2026. Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-dont-speed-up-when-overtaken.fact: Georgian traffic law (Article 34): the driver being overtaken must not hinder the overtaking by speeding up or by any other action; and if a driver has to abort an overtake and wants to return to their lane, the drivers behind must let them back in.
ge-dont-speed-up-when-overtaken.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald), consolidated version of 25/06/2026. Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-slow-and-long-leave-gap.fact: Georgian traffic law (Article 34): outside built-up areas, on a road with only one lane in each direction, a driver going slower than the allowed maximum and a driver of a vehicle or combination longer than 7 m must, except while starting or carrying out an overtake, keep such a gap to the vehicle ahead that an overtaking vehicle can safely pull in in front of them; this does not apply in heavy traffic or where overtaking is banned.
ge-slow-and-long-leave-gap.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald), consolidated version of 25/06/2026. Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-no-harsh-braking.fact: Georgian traffic law (Article 33): a driver is forbidden to brake harshly except when braking is needed to avoid a crash; a driver who means to slow down noticeably without an immediate danger must first make sure this will not endanger or unduly hinder others.
ge-no-harsh-braking.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald), consolidated version of 25/06/2026. Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-no-overtaking-blind-crest.fact: Georgian traffic law (Article 34, with the definition in Article 5): overtaking by moving into the oncoming lane is banned in limited visibility, which the law defines as a short bend, the top of a rise, greenery, roadside structures or an obstacle that cuts the view ahead so much that driving at the allowed maximum speed could be dangerous.
ge-no-overtaking-blind-crest.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald), consolidated version of 25/06/2026. Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-rain-start-slippery.fact: Georgian traffic law (Article 25) lists, among things a driver must take into account: when rain begins, the road surface turns muddy and slippery, so the driver should reduce speed by braking smoothly.
ge-rain-start-slippery.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald), consolidated version of 25/06/2026. Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-high-speed-dulls-sense.fact: Georgian traffic law (Article 25) warns that driving at high speed for a long time lowers concentration and dulls the sense of high speed.
ge-high-speed-dulls-sense.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald), consolidated version of 25/06/2026. Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

hc-skid-steer-into-skid.fact: UK Highway Code rule 119: skids are usually caused by braking, accelerating or steering too harshly, or by driving too fast for the conditions; if one starts, remove the cause by fully releasing the brake pedal or easing off the accelerator, and turn the steering wheel in the direction of the skid: if the rear of the car slides to the right, steer right at once.
hc-skid-steer-into-skid.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-brake-early-lightly.fact: UK Highway Code rule 117: in normal driving the safest way to brake is early and lightly, braking more firmly as you begin to stop, then easing the pressure just before the car comes to rest to avoid a jerky stop.
hc-brake-early-lightly.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-hill-parking-wheels.fact: UK Highway Code rule 252: when parking on a hill, park close to the kerb and apply the handbrake firmly; facing uphill, select a forward gear and turn the steering wheel away from the kerb; facing downhill, select reverse and turn the wheel towards the kerb; in an automatic, use 'park'.
hc-hill-parking-wheels.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-trailer-snaking.fact: UK Highway Code rule 98: if a trailer starts to swerve or snake, or you lose control, ease off the accelerator and reduce speed gently to regain control; do not brake harshly. Spread the load evenly with heavy items over the axle(s) and a downward load on the tow ball, within the maker's limits.
hc-trailer-snaking.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-wind-gusts.fact: UK Highway Code rule 232: high-sided vehicles are most affected by windy weather, but strong gusts can also blow a car, cyclist, motorcyclist or horse rider off course, especially on open stretches exposed to strong crosswinds, when passing bridges, or at gaps in hedges; rule 233: in very windy weather large vehicles create turbulence that can affect smaller ones.
hc-wind-gusts.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-animals-slow-no-horn.fact: UK Highway Code rule 214: when passing animals, drive slowly, give them plenty of room and be ready to stop; do not scare them by sounding the horn, revving the engine or accelerating hard once past; keep speed down at bends and on narrow country roads; if a herd blocks the road, stop and switch off the engine until they have left it.
hc-animals-slow-no-horn.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-cyclist-1-5-metres.fact: UK Highway Code rule 163: when overtaking, leave at least 1.5 m to cyclists at speeds up to 30 mph (about 48 km/h) and more at higher speeds; pass horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles below 10 mph leaving at least 2 m, and pedestrians walking in the road at least 2 m at low speed; if these clearances are impossible, wait behind.
hc-cyclist-1-5-metres.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-drop-back-behind-lorry.fact: UK Highway Code rule 164: overtaking large vehicles is harder; drop back, which improves your view ahead and lets the driver see you in their mirrors; getting too close hides the road ahead; it takes longer to pass a large vehicle, so make sure you have room before committing, and if in doubt do not overtake.
hc-drop-back-behind-lorry.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-large-vehicles-need-room.fact: UK Highway Code rule 221: large vehicles may need extra road space to turn or to deal with a hazard you cannot see; if you follow a bus or articulated lorry, its driver may not be able to see you in the mirrors; be prepared to stop and wait if it needs room or time to turn.
hc-large-vehicles-need-room.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-silent-tyres-on-ice.fact: UK Highway Code rule 231: when travelling on ice, tyres make virtually no noise; steering that feels unresponsive may indicate ice.
hc-silent-tyres-on-ice.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

on-hands-nine-and-three.fact: Ontario's official driver's handbook (Ministry of Transportation): picture the steering wheel as a clock and place your hands at nine o'clock and three o'clock.
on-hands-nine-and-three.licence_note: Government of Ontario, Official MTO Driver's Handbook (copyright King's Printer for Ontario). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

on-mirrors-every-5-seconds.fact: Ontario's official driver's handbook: check your mirrors every five seconds or so, and check blind spots by turning your head to look over your shoulder; be extra careful at dusk and dawn when everyone struggles with changing light.
on-mirrors-every-5-seconds.licence_note: Government of Ontario, Official MTO Driver's Handbook (copyright King's Printer for Ontario). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

on-wheels-straight-before-left-turn.fact: Ontario's official driver's handbook (right-hand traffic, like Georgia): when stopped at an intersection waiting for oncoming traffic to clear before a left turn, don't turn the steering wheel to the left until you can complete the turn, because with the wheels turned left your vehicle could be pushed into the path of oncoming traffic.
on-wheels-straight-before-left-turn.licence_note: Government of Ontario, Official MTO Driver's Handbook (copyright King's Printer for Ontario). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

on-brake-before-the-turn.fact: Ontario's official driver's handbook: slow down before you enter a turn, the sharper the turn the slower you should go; to keep full control, finish braking before you turn the steering wheel.
on-brake-before-the-turn.licence_note: Government of Ontario, Official MTO Driver's Handbook (copyright King's Printer for Ontario). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

on-fog-low-beams.fact: Ontario's official driver's handbook: in fog use low-beam headlights, because high beams reflect off the moisture droplets in the fog and make it harder to see (in blowing snow they reflect off the ice particles); use fog lights too if fitted, and use the right edge of the road as a guide rather than the centre line.
on-fog-low-beams.licence_note: Government of Ontario, Official MTO Driver's Handbook (copyright King's Printer for Ontario). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

on-glare-look-right.fact: Ontario's official driver's handbook: when meeting oncoming vehicles with bright headlights at night, look up and beyond and slightly to the right of the oncoming lights.
on-glare-look-right.licence_note: Government of Ontario, Official MTO Driver's Handbook (copyright King's Printer for Ontario). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

on-tunnel-sunglasses-off.fact: Ontario's official driver's handbook: when you enter a tunnel on a bright day, slow down to let your eyes adjust to the reduced light, remove your sunglasses and turn on your headlights.
on-tunnel-sunglasses-off.licence_note: Government of Ontario, Official MTO Driver's Handbook (copyright King's Printer for Ontario). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

on-tyre-blowout.fact: Ontario's official driver's handbook: a tyre blowout can cause tremendous steering and wheel vibration, but don't be alarmed; take your foot off the gas pedal to slow down, steer the vehicle firmly in the direction you want to go, and bring it to a stop off the road.
on-tyre-blowout.licence_note: Government of Ontario, Official MTO Driver's Handbook (copyright King's Printer for Ontario). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

on-wheels-off-pavement.fact: Ontario's official driver's handbook: if your wheels go off the pavement, don't panic; grip the steering wheel firmly, take your foot off the gas, avoid heavy braking, and once the vehicle is under control steer back toward the pavement, ready to correct the steering when the wheels are fully back on.
on-wheels-off-pavement.licence_note: Government of Ontario, Official MTO Driver's Handbook (copyright King's Printer for Ontario). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

on-truck-mirror-face.fact: Ontario's official driver's handbook: large commercial vehicles have big blind spots on both sides and directly behind; if you can't see the driver's face in the large vehicle's side mirror, the driver cannot see you; after passing a large vehicle don't cut in closely in front of it, because it needs much more distance to stop.
on-truck-mirror-face.licence_note: Government of Ontario, Official MTO Driver's Handbook (copyright King's Printer for Ontario). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

on-trailer-load-front.fact: Ontario's official driver's handbook: generally more of a trailer's load should be in front of the trailer axle than behind it; about 5 to 10 per cent of the trailer's total weight should rest on the hitch, within the hitch's marked limit; poor load balance can make the trailer sway or fishtail, and too much weight at the rear can even separate the ball and hitch.
on-trailer-load-front.licence_note: Government of Ontario, Official MTO Driver's Handbook (copyright King's Printer for Ontario). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

on-trailer-reverse-steer-opposite.fact: Ontario's official driver's handbook: to back a trailer to the right, steer to the left (the front of the trailer goes left and its rear goes right); to back to the left, steer to the right. Back up very slowly in small steering movements, ideally with someone outside guiding you, and practise in an empty parking lot.
on-trailer-reverse-steer-opposite.licence_note: Government of Ontario, Official MTO Driver's Handbook (copyright King's Printer for Ontario). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

sgi-collision-course-looks-still.fact: Saskatchewan Driver's Handbook (SGI): a vehicle on a collision course with you appears stationary in your peripheral vision, so turn your head to check an approaching vehicle rather than relying on side vision alone.
sgi-collision-course-looks-still.licence_note: Saskatchewan Government Insurance (SGI) Driver's Handbook (copyright SGI). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

sgi-steer-where-you-look.fact: Saskatchewan Driver's Handbook (SGI): you steer where you look; to drive straight, look about 12 seconds ahead, and in an emergency look where you want to go and steer there.
sgi-steer-where-you-look.licence_note: Saskatchewan Government Insurance (SGI) Driver's Handbook (copyright SGI). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

mpi-gravel-six-seconds.fact: Manitoba Public Insurance driver's handbook: on gravel roads stay at least six seconds behind other vehicles, more on rough or loose surfaces, because dust clouds can block your view, and stopping distances are longer on loose gravel.
mpi-gravel-six-seconds.licence_note: Manitoba Public Insurance Driver's Handbook (copyright MPI, a Manitoba Crown corporation). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

qld-braking-distance-quadruples.fact: Queensland Government stopping-distance table (dry road, average family car): braking distance is 14 m from 50 km/h and 56 m from 100 km/h, so twice the speed needs four times the braking distance; with a 1.5 s reaction the total stopping distance is 35 m and 98 m.
qld-braking-distance-quadruples.licence_note: Queensland Government (qld.gov.au), Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (credit: © The State of Queensland). Restated in our own words.

qld-reaction-distance.fact: Queensland Government: in an emergency the average driver takes about 1.5 seconds to react; in that time a car covers 21 m at 50 km/h and 42 m at 100 km/h before braking even begins (dry-road table).
qld-reaction-distance.licence_note: Queensland Government (qld.gov.au), Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (credit: © The State of Queensland). Restated in our own words.

qld-seven-kmh-hits-at-30.fact: Queensland Government stopping-distances page (video presented by Prof. Barry Watson, Director of CARRS-Q, QUT): a car braking suddenly from 60 km/h stops in time; the same car at 67 km/h, braking at the exact same point, still hits at about 30 km/h.
qld-seven-kmh-hits-at-30.licence_note: Queensland Government (qld.gov.au), Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (credit: © The State of Queensland). Restated in our own words.

mt-overtaking-takes-19-seconds.fact: Montana Office of Public Instruction driver-education fact sheet: starting from two seconds behind and making a flying pass, overtaking a vehicle doing 30 mph at 40 mph takes about 13 seconds, one doing 40 mph at 50 mph about 16 seconds, and one doing 50 mph (about 80 km/h) at 60 mph (about 97 km/h) about 19 seconds.
mt-overtaking-takes-19-seconds.licence_note: Montana Office of Public Instruction driver-education fact sheet (US state government material). Only the figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

aaa-halogen-low-beams-speed.fact: AAA tests (May 2015): halogen headlights, then on over 80% of US cars, may fail to light unlit roads well enough to stop safely at speeds as low as 40 mph (about 64 km/h); halogen high beams improved sight distance by 28% in tests but in real conditions may only allow safe stopping up to about 48 mph (about 77 km/h).
aaa-halogen-low-beams-speed.licence_note: AAA newsroom press release (copyright AAA). Only the findings and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

nws-30cm-water-carries-car.fact: US National Weather Service: 12 inches (about 30 cm) of rushing water can carry away most cars and 2 feet (about 60 cm) can carry away SUVs and trucks; over half of all flood-related drownings happen when a vehicle is driven into hazardous flood water, and the road under the water may have collapsed.
nws-30cm-water-carries-car.licence_note: US federal government work (National Weather Service), public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

aa-flood-10cm-rule.fact: The AA (UK): don't drive into flood water that is moving or more than 10 cm (4 inches) deep; if you must cross, let oncoming cars pass first and drive slowly and steadily (about 3-4 mph) so you don't make a bow wave, using higher revs than usual, and test your brakes afterwards; an egg cup of water sucked into the engine can cause significant damage, and on many cars the air intake is low at the front.
aa-flood-10cm-rule.licence_note: The AA (UK motoring organisation) advice page (copyright AA). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

adac-microsleep-56m.fact: ADAC: during a microsleep of just two seconds at 100 km/h a car travels 56 m uncontrolled; acute warning signs of tiredness include frequent yawning, sudden chills and a strong urge to move; ADAC advises a break every two hours and, when tired, a nap of 10 to 20 minutes.
adac-microsleep-56m.licence_note: ADAC e.V. press release (copyright ADAC). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

adac-afternoon-dip.fact: ADAC: the body has a biological low between 2 and 5 am and again in the afternoon around 2 pm, so driving at these times works against the body clock.
adac-afternoon-dip.licence_note: ADAC e.V. press release (copyright ADAC). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

ny-drowsy-myths.fact: New York State Governor's Traffic Safety Committee: opening the windows, turning up the radio or turning on the air conditioner will not keep you awake while driving; caffeine is only a short fix that takes about 30 minutes to be felt and can wear off quickly; a drowsy driver should pull over in a well-lit area and take a 20-minute nap.
ny-drowsy-myths.licence_note: New York State Governor's Traffic Safety Committee page (US state government). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

cdc-17-hours-awake.fact: CDC (NIOSH): being awake for 17 hours is similar to having a blood alcohol concentration of 0.05%, and being awake for 24 hours is similar to 0.10%.
cdc-17-hours-awake.licence_note: US federal government work (CDC/NIOSH), public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

nrcan-steady-speed.fact: Natural Resources Canada: varying your speed up and down between 75 and 85 km/h every 18 seconds can increase fuel use by 20%; keep a steady speed (cruise control on highways when conditions allow).
nrcan-steady-speed.licence_note: Government of Canada (Natural Resources Canada) page; its terms allow free non-commercial reproduction, so only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

nrcan-gentle-start.fact: Natural Resources Canada: accelerate gently, taking about 5 seconds to reach 20 km/h from a stop; this is one of the techniques that together can cut fuel use and CO2 by as much as 25%.
nrcan-gentle-start.licence_note: Government of Canada (Natural Resources Canada) page; its terms allow free non-commercial reproduction, so only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

continental-understeer.fact: Continental (tyre maker): understeer is when the front tyres lose grip and the car turns less than the driver steers, often with screeching tyres; front-wheel-drive cars are more prone to it (rear-wheel-drive to oversteer); it is usually caused by entering a corner too fast or turning too sharply. If it happens, don't turn the wheel harder: ease the steering so the front tyres regain grip, gently lift off the accelerator and don't slam on the brakes.
continental-understeer.licence_note: Continental Tyres UK tyre-knowledge page (copyright Continental). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

nissan-hill-start-2s.fact: Nissan owner's manual (X-Trail, 2024): hill start assist holds the brakes for a maximum of 2 seconds after the driver releases the brake pedal on a hill; after 2 seconds the vehicle begins to roll back and the system stops; never rely on it alone, as it is not designed to hold the vehicle at a standstill.
nissan-hill-start-2s.licence_note: Nissan owner's manual online (copyright Nissan). Only the technical fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

nps-brake-smell-descent.fact: US National Park Service (Rocky Mountain National Park): use lower gears downhill to slow the car without wearing down the brakes; if you smell your brakes, pull over, let them cool and test them before going on; don't drive if the brakes are not working properly.
nps-brake-smell-descent.licence_note: US federal government work (National Park Service), public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

oil-dipstick-how-to-read.fact: The AA's way to check engine oil: park on level ground (a slope gives a misleading reading), check with the engine cold or wait 5 to 10 minutes after a drive, pull the dipstick out, wipe it clean, push it fully back in, pull it out again and read where the oil mark sits; between the minimum and maximum marks is fine.
oil-dipstick-how-to-read.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) advice page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

oil-dipstick-litre-gap.fact: According to the AA, the difference between the minimum and maximum marks on a dipstick is about one litre of oil, and putting too much oil in is just as bad as having too little.
oil-dipstick-litre-gap.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) advice page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

oil-change-yearly-low-mileage.fact: AAA says engine oil should be changed at least once a year even if the car has not reached the mileage interval.
oil-change-yearly-low-mileage.licence_note: AAA (American Automobile Association) advice page, copyright AAA. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as AAA's advice.

severe-service-conditions.fact: AAA: for cars that follow a mileage-based maintenance schedule (cars with an oil-life monitoring system shorten the interval automatically), 'severe service' driving calls for the shorter schedule with more frequent oil changes: primarily short trips of 5 miles (about 8 km) or less; extremely hot, cold or dusty climates; sustained stop-and-go driving; carrying heavy loads or towing a trailer.
severe-service-conditions.licence_note: AAA (American Automobile Association) advice page, copyright AAA. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as AAA's list.

oil-top-up-mixing.fact: ADAC: oils made for the same engine concept can generally be mixed, synthetic with mineral oil too; petrol-engine and diesel-engine oils should not be mixed, and two-stroke oil does not belong in a four-stroke car engine. The carmaker's required specification must always be met: an oil below it can cause damage, while topping up with a higher-grade oil is unproblematic.
oil-top-up-mixing.licence_note: ADAC (adac.de) page in German, copyright ADAC e.V. Only the fact is used, translated and restated in our own words, no text copied; said as ADAC's advice.

oil-opened-bottle-shelf-life.fact: ADAC: manufacturers recommend storing unopened engine oil for three to at most five years; an opened container should be kept for at most half a year, because air and moisture get in.
oil-opened-bottle-shelf-life.licence_note: ADAC (adac.de) page in German, copyright ADAC e.V. Only the fact is used, translated and restated in our own words, no text copied; said as ADAC's advice.

oil-diesel-level-rises.fact: ADAC: in diesel cars with a particulate filter the oil level can rise, because fuel gets into the oil (fuel dilution), and the diluted oil lubricates worse.
oil-diesel-level-rises.licence_note: ADAC (adac.de) page in German, copyright ADAC e.V. Only the fact is used, translated and restated in our own words, no text copied; said as ADAC's statement.

brake-fluid-level-pad-wear.fact: Haynes: as brake pads wear, the caliper pistons extend further and displace more fluid, so the level in the reservoir drops; a low level points either to worn pads or to a leak in the lines, calipers or wheel cylinders, and a leak needs inspection as soon as possible.
brake-fluid-level-pad-wear.licence_note: Haynes (repair-manual publisher) tutorial page, copyright Haynes. Only the technical fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

brake-fluid-change-interval.fact: Textar (a brake maker) says brake fluid is usually replaced around every 2 to 3 years or every 30,000 miles, whichever comes first, though manufacturers' intervals differ; fluid that has turned a muddy brown is a good sign it is time.
brake-fluid-change-interval.licence_note: Textar (brake manufacturer) knowledge page, copyright TMD Friction / Textar. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as Textar's guidance.

coolant-check-cold.fact: The AA advises checking engine coolant only when the engine has been switched off for at least 30 minutes (longer if it has overheated); the coolant should sit between the min and max marks on the side of the expansion tank, and it is worth checking every couple of weeks.
coolant-check-cold.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) advice page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

coolant-should-not-drop.fact: RAC: most modern cooling systems are sealed and do not need topping up; a coolant level that repeatedly falls below the guide marks usually indicates a leak.
coolant-should-not-drop.licence_note: RAC (rac.co.uk) advice page, copyright RAC Motoring Services. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's statement.

spark-plug-iridium-not-equal.fact: NGK: its OE-style Laser Iridium plugs (iridium centre tip, platinum ground electrode) are typically designed to last 80,000 to 100,000 miles, while its single-precious-metal Iridium IX plugs are designed to last 40,000 to 50,000 miles, so 'iridium' on the box does not by itself tell the interval.
spark-plug-iridium-not-equal.licence_note: NGK Spark Plugs (Niterra) resource page, manufacturer information, copyright NGK / Niterra. Only the figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as NGK's figures.

bulb-dont-touch-glass.fact: RAC: when fitting a new halogen headlight bulb, avoid touching the glass with bare fingers, because oils from the skin can create hot spots that may shorten the bulb's life or cause premature failure.
bulb-dont-touch-glass.licence_note: RAC (rac.co.uk) advice page, copyright RAC Motoring Services. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's advice.

bulbs-replace-in-pairs.fact: RAC: if one headlight bulb has failed, consider replacing the bulb on the opposite side at the same time, because bulbs often have similar lifespans and the second may be near the end of its life too.
bulbs-replace-in-pairs.licence_note: RAC (rac.co.uk) advice page, copyright RAC Motoring Services. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's advice.

indicator-flash-rate.fact: Hella: indicators flash at a frequency between 60 and 120 times per minute, and the flasher unit has a current-dependent control circuit that changes the flashing frequency when a lamp fails.
indicator-flash-rate.licence_note: HELLA Tech World page, manufacturer technical information, copyright HELLA / FORVIA. Only the technical fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

check-lights-alone-reflection.fact: RAC: lights are easier to check with a helper, but alone you can use reflections on walls or other cars to get a rough idea of what is working; go through side lights, dipped beam, main beam, fog lights, indicators, brake lights, reversing lights and hazards, and replace any that fail.
check-lights-alone-reflection.licence_note: RAC (rac.co.uk) advice page, copyright RAC Motoring Services. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's advice.

headlamp-levelling-load.fact: Hella: the vehicle's load changes the range of the headlamps and may dazzle other road users, which is why headlamp levelling has been legally required on new vehicles since 1993 (76/756/EEC, ECE R48); with manual systems the driver adjusts the beam angle with a switch, and many loaded vehicles dazzle oncoming traffic because drivers don't know how their adjustment works.
headlamp-levelling-load.licence_note: HELLA Tech World page, manufacturer technical information, copyright HELLA / FORVIA. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

wiper-blades-6-12-months.fact: AAA: wiper blades are generally recommended to be replaced every 6 to 12 months depending on climate and driving conditions; high heat makes the rubber warp, harden and crack, cold makes it stiff and brittle, and signs of wear include streaking, skipping or chattering, noise and unwiped spots.
wiper-blades-6-12-months.licence_note: AAA club (Auto Club Group) advice page, copyright AAA. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as AAA's advice.

mot-washer-fluid-fail.fact: UK MOT inspection manual: windscreen washers must provide enough fluid for the wipers to clear the windscreen effectively; washers not working or not providing sufficient fluid is a major defect, as is a wiper not operating.
mot-washer-fluid-fail.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words; a UK rule, said as the UK's.

mot-windscreen-chip-size.fact: UK MOT inspection manual: testers check for windscreen damage more than 10 mm across in zone A (a 290 mm wide part of the wiper-swept area centred on the steering wheel) and more than 40 mm across in the rest of the swept area; damage that affects the driver's view of the road is a major defect (a fail), failure being justified only if it significantly affects the view, while damage that does not affect the view is a minor defect.
mot-windscreen-chip-size.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words; a UK rule, said as the UK's.

fuse-colour-code.fact: RAC: blade fuses are colour-coded by rating (5 A tan, 10 A red, 15 A blue, 20 A yellow, 25 A clear, 30 A green); hold a removed fuse up to the light, and if the thin metal strip inside is broken or burnt it has blown; replace it only with one of the same amperage.
fuse-colour-code.licence_note: RAC (rac.co.uk) advice page, copyright RAC Motoring Services. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's advice.

fuse-blows-again.fact: RAC: if a replacement fuse blows again, it signals a deeper electrical issue that needs professional attention from a mechanic.
fuse-blows-again.licence_note: RAC (rac.co.uk) advice page, copyright RAC Motoring Services. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's advice.

battery-half-of-breakdowns.fact: ADAC 2025 breakdown figures (Germany): problems with the car battery caused 45.4% of ADAC road patrol (Straßenwacht) call-outs, far ahead of engine and engine management at 21.8% and generator, starter, on-board electrics and lighting at 10.4%; ADAC recorded 3,691,813 call-outs in total in 2025.
battery-half-of-breakdowns.licence_note: ADAC (adac.de) corporate news page in German, copyright ADAC e.V. Only the figures are used, translated and restated in our own words, no text copied; said as ADAC's statistics for Germany.

ev-12v-battery-breakdowns.fact: ADAC 2024: for electric cars too, a defective starter battery (the small 12 V battery) was the most common cause of breakdowns, at 50 percent of call-outs.
ev-12v-battery-breakdowns.licence_note: ADAC press release in German, copyright ADAC e.V. Only the figure is used, translated and restated in our own words, no text copied; said as ADAC's statistics for Germany.

battery-3-5-year-guarantee.fact: AA: most car batteries have a guarantee of 3 to 5 years, so after that you are living on borrowed time and should consider replacing an older battery before it fails.
battery-3-5-year-guarantee.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) advice page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

battery-short-trips-flat.fact: AA: flat batteries are commonly caused by a lack of use or too many short journeys; if you rarely drive far, charging the battery overnight every 2 weeks or so keeps it charged.
battery-short-trips-flat.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) advice page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

battery-12-4-volts-recharge.fact: VARTA: a fully charged starter battery has a voltage of 12.8 V, and if its open-circuit voltage drops below 12.4 V the battery needs to be recharged.
battery-12-4-volts-recharge.licence_note: VARTA Automotive (Clarios) knowledge page, battery-maker information, copyright VARTA / Clarios. Only the figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as VARTA's figures.

battery-headlight-dim-test.fact: VARTA: if the headlights quickly become darker when the engine is switched off, the battery should be charged as soon as possible.
battery-headlight-dim-test.licence_note: VARTA Automotive (Clarios) knowledge page, battery-maker information, copyright VARTA / Clarios. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as VARTA's advice.

start-stop-battery-type.fact: VARTA: a start-stop car's battery can only be replaced with a battery of the same type (an AGM car needs AGM; an EFB car can take EFB or an AGM upgrade); fitting a normal battery instead leads to rapid deterioration and an inevitable breakdown.
start-stop-battery-type.licence_note: VARTA Automotive (Clarios) knowledge page, battery-maker information, copyright VARTA / Clarios. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as VARTA's advice.

start-stop-off-low-battery.fact: VARTA: when the battery has only a low charge, the battery management system switches the start-stop function off so the engine can still be started (it can also pause for very high or low temperatures or heavy fan or AC demand); if start-stop fails often or never activates, a workshop battery test is advised.
start-stop-off-low-battery.licence_note: VARTA Automotive (Clarios) knowledge page, battery-maker information, copyright VARTA / Clarios. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as VARTA's statement.

battery-disconnect-negative-first.fact: RAC: when disconnecting a car battery, always disconnect the negative terminal first; when reconnecting, always start with the positive terminal.
battery-disconnect-negative-first.licence_note: RAC (rac.co.uk) advice page, copyright RAC Motoring Services. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's advice.

dashboard-light-colours.fact: AA: dashboard warning lights follow colours: red means take immediate action and you shouldn't drive the car, amber often means something needs checking by a garage, and green means a system is on and everything is OK.
dashboard-light-colours.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) advice page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

oil-pressure-light-not-level.fact: AA: the oil warning light shows a loss of oil pressure in the engine; stop as soon as possible and check the oil level, and if the light is on while the level is right there is a problem with the oil supply (such as a faulty pump or blocked filter): turn the engine off and call for breakdown help.
