oil-pressure-light-not-level.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) advice page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

battery-light-charging-fault.fact: AA: if the red battery light comes on while driving, there may be a problem with the wiring, the alternator or the alternator drive belt (or simply a flat battery); stop somewhere safe, turn the engine off and don't restart it, as that could make the problem worse.
battery-light-charging-fault.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) advice page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

glow-plug-light-wait.fact: AA: on a diesel, the glow plug light shows the engine's glow plugs are warming up, and it is not recommended to start the engine until this light goes out.
glow-plug-light-wait.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) advice page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

brake-and-abs-lights-together.fact: AA: if the brake and ABS warning lights come on at the same time, there could be a major fault with the brakes: stop and call for breakdown help; with the brake light alone, first check the handbrake is fully released, then check and top up the brake fluid.
brake-and-abs-lights-together.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) advice page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

esp-light-flashing-normal.fact: AA: an ESP (stability control) light flashing on wet or slippery roads is normal and shows the system is working; if it stays on in normal conditions, get it checked.
esp-light-flashing-normal.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) advice page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

adblue-empty-no-restart.fact: AA: AdBlue (32.5% urea, 67.5% de-ionised water) is used at typically around a litre every 600 miles (about 1,000 km); if the AdBlue tank runs empty you won't be able to restart the engine once it is switched off (about 5 litres should be enough to restart); it usually has a small blue filler cap next to the diesel filler, and putting it in the fuel tank can cause expensive damage to the tank, pump and injection system.
adblue-empty-no-restart.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) advice page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

wheel-change-loosen-first.fact: Michelin: loosen the wheel nuts slightly before raising the vehicle with the jack, which stops the wheel from spinning when you apply force.
wheel-change-loosen-first.licence_note: Michelin (michelinman.com) advice page, copyright Michelin. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as Michelin's advice.

jack-never-under-car.fact: AAA: never put your body under the car while it is raised on the jack, and place wheel wedges (or large rocks or sticks) around the tyres, or at least the tyre on the opposite corner from the flat.
jack-never-under-car.licence_note: AAA (American Automobile Association) advice page, copyright AAA. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as AAA's advice.

wheel-nuts-star-pattern.fact: Michelin: when refitting a wheel, tighten the nuts in a cross pattern (each nut, then the one opposite) rather than in a circle.
wheel-nuts-star-pattern.licence_note: Michelin (michelinman.com) advice page, copyright Michelin. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as Michelin's advice.

wheel-retorque-50km.fact: Continental: during the first 50 to 100 km after a tyre change the wheel settles, which can reduce the clamping force of the nuts, so garages and tyre dealers typically re-torque the wheels about 50 km after a tyre change, often free.
wheel-retorque-50km.licence_note: Continental tyre-knowledge page, manufacturer information, copyright Continental AG. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as Continental's advice.

no-wheel-change-motorway.fact: RAC (UK): you should never attempt to change a tyre on the motorway; stop on the hard shoulder, get everyone out through the doors away from the traffic (the left-hand doors in the UK) and contact your breakdown provider.
no-wheel-change-motorway.licence_note: RAC (rac.co.uk) advice page, copyright RAC Motoring Services. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's (UK) advice.

space-saver-limits.fact: TyreSafe: a space-saver spare is usually limited to 50 mph (about 80 km/h), and that in dry conditions; it is recommended for no more than 50 miles (about 80 km); it should be inflated to 60 psi (about 4.1 bar), and its pressure and condition should be checked regularly.
space-saver-limits.licence_note: TyreSafe (UK tyre-safety charity) advice page, copyright TyreSafe. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as TyreSafe's advice.

run-flat-50-miles-tpms.fact: Goodyear: after a puncture, run-flat tyres let the driver continue for 50 miles (about 80 km) at around 50 mph (about 80 km/h) unless the vehicle handbook says otherwise; because their construction counteracts the stability issues that normally alert a driver to a puncture, the vehicle must have a tyre pressure monitoring system.
run-flat-50-miles-tpms.licence_note: Goodyear (goodyear.eu) advice page, manufacturer information, copyright Goodyear. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as Goodyear's guidance.

run-flat-markings-replace.fact: RAC: run-flat tyres can be identified by sidewall markings such as Run-Flat, SSR, RFT or ROF (or an ISO symbol: a circle with the letters RSC), and the RAC recommends replacing a punctured run-flat tyre rather than attempting a repair.
run-flat-markings-replace.licence_note: RAC (rac.co.uk) advice page, copyright RAC Motoring Services. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's guidance.

new-cars-no-spare.fact: RAC research published 20 November 2023: of 313 new car models on sale in the UK, only 8 (2.6%, rounded to 3%) came with any form of spare wheel as standard; on many others a spare is an optional extra.
new-cars-no-spare.licence_note: RAC (rac.co.uk) advice page, copyright RAC Motoring Services. Only the figure is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's (UK) research.

puncture-repair-zone.fact: Continental: a tyre puncture is unrepairable if it is 6 mm or more in diameter, and repairs are limited to the central three-quarters of the tread; sidewall damage is never repairable; and driving on a deflated tyre is extremely dangerous and can ruin one that was repairable.
puncture-repair-zone.licence_note: Continental tyre-knowledge page, manufacturer information, copyright Continental AG. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as Continental's guidance.

puncture-kit-temporary.fact: TyreSafe: emergency tyre puncture repair kits offer a temporary fix in four out of five punctures, should only be used if it is safe to do so, and should only ever be a temporary measure.
puncture-kit-temporary.licence_note: TyreSafe (UK tyre-safety charity) advice page, copyright TyreSafe. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as TyreSafe's advice.

dish-soap-car-wash.fact: Consumer Reports: don't wash a car with household cleaning agents such as dishwashing detergent, hand soap or glass cleaner, which can strip the protective wax; use a car-wash product, and don't wash when the body is hot, because heat dries soap and water too quickly and can leave spots.
dish-soap-car-wash.licence_note: Consumer Reports article, copyright Consumer Reports. Only the advice is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as Consumer Reports' advice.

two-bucket-wash.fact: RAC: wash using the two-bucket method, one bucket of shampoo solution and one of plain water for rinsing the mitt; start at the top, where the car is usually cleanest, and work down; dry with a microfibre towel, because leaving the car to air-dry increases water spots and streaks.
two-bucket-wash.licence_note: RAC (rac.co.uk) advice page, copyright RAC Motoring Services. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's advice.

bird-droppings-heat.fact: Autoglym's own tests: the etching left by bird droppings is not mainly due to their acidity (substitutes of different acidity showed negligible differences), but to the paint's lacquer, softened by the sun, contracting and moulding to the uneven dried deposit as it cools; remove droppings as soon as possible, softening dried ones under a moist cloth for about ten minutes.
bird-droppings-heat.licence_note: Autoglym (car-care maker) blog reporting its own research, copyright Autoglym. Only the finding is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as Autoglym's test result.

road-salt-underbody-wash.fact: AA: salt can be a major accelerator of rust, so occasionally pressure-wash the car's underside, especially in the winter months when roads are salted.
road-salt-underbody-wash.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) car-care page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

stone-chips-rust.fact: AA: road salt and stone chips can still cause problems, particularly if minor damage is ignored; for deeper scratches, get a paint touch-up pen from a dealer to ensure an exact colour match.
stone-chips-rust.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) car-care page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

car-mould-condensation.fact: AA: the main cause of mould in a car is condensation, often linked to loose or damaged door and window seals; signs of seal problems include draughts, wind noise inside the car while driving, or wet carpets or seats.
car-mould-condensation.licence_note: AA (theaa.com) car-care page, copyright The Automobile Association. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the AA's advice.

ac-use-regularly.fact: RAC: air-con systems inevitably leak refrigerant gas over time, particularly if they aren't used regularly.
ac-use-regularly.licence_note: RAC (rac.co.uk) advice page, copyright RAC Motoring Services. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's statement.

braking-pulls-one-side.fact: UK Highway Code (Annex 6): if the vehicle pulls to one side when braking, it is most likely a brake fault or incorrectly inflated tyres; consult a garage or mechanic immediately.
braking-pulls-one-side.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words; UK advice, said as the UK's.

unusual-smells-investigate.fact: UK Highway Code (Annex 6): if your vehicle smells of anything unusual, such as burning rubber, petrol or an electrical fault, investigate immediately and do not risk a fire.
unusual-smells-investigate.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words; UK advice, said as the UK's.

copart-run-and-drive.fact: Copart's 'Run and Drive' label only means that when the car arrived at Copart's yard, Copart checked that it started, could be put into gear and moved forward under its own power. Copart does not guarantee that it is roadworthy or can be driven lawfully, or that it will still start and move when it is picked up (the battery can die, or a salvage car can deteriorate while it waits in the yard).
copart-run-and-drive.licence_note: Copart's own terminology page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as Copart's definition. The same definition is on https://www.copart.com/content/us/en/landing-page/smart-buying/common-misconceptions (opened the same day).

copart-engine-start.fact: Copart's 'Engine Start Program' label means only that, when the car arrived at Copart's facility, Copart verified that the engine started and ran at idle. It says nothing about the car moving or driving, and Copart does not guarantee that it will still start or idle when it is picked up.
copart-engine-start.licence_note: Copart's own terminology page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as Copart's definition.

copart-damage-codes-equal.fact: On Copart listings damage codes appear as 'Primary Damage' and 'Secondary Damage'; Copart says both carry significant information and neither should be read as more important than the other. The codes show only known or reported damage, Copart expressly disclaims their accuracy, and it strongly recommends inspecting a lot before buying.
copart-damage-codes-equal.licence_note: Copart help centre page (copyrighted, updated 2024-11-11): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied. The same text is in Copart's glossary, https://www.copart.com/help/finding-vehicles/glossary-of-common-terms-used-at-copart.

copart-flood-cars-dried.fact: Copart's 'Water/Flood' damage type covers anything from water rising just enough to wet the floor to a fully submerged car, including cars recovered from hurricanes, and in many cases Copart treats these cars to extract the water and try to prevent mould, fungus and bad odours.
copart-flood-cars-dried.licence_note: Copart help centre page (copyrighted, updated 2024-11-11): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

copart-odometer-brands.fact: Copart lists every odometer reading with one of four descriptions: ACTUAL (believed to be the true mileage), NOT ACTUAL (the reading is wrong or the true mileage cannot be known), EXEMPT (federal law does not require an odometer code for that lot) and EXCEEDS MECHANICAL LIMITS (the car went past the odometer's maximum and it started again from 0).
copart-odometer-brands.licence_note: Copart help centre glossary (copyrighted, updated 2025-11-25): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

copart-retail-value-pre-damage.fact: Copart's 'Estimated Retail Value' is the figure submitted by the seller, and for a damaged lot it is the car's value before the damage happened; Copart makes no representation that it is valid or accurate.
copart-retail-value-pre-damage.licence_note: Copart help centre glossary (copyrighted, updated 2025-11-25): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

copart-engine-from-vin.fact: On Copart the listed engine is the specification denoted by the car's VIN, not a confirmation of what is under the bonnet; Copart encourages buyers to inspect the vehicle to verify whether the original equipment is present at the time of sale.
copart-engine-from-vin.licence_note: Copart help centre glossary (copyrighted, updated 2025-11-25): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

copart-mostly-salvage-as-is.fact: Copart says most vehicles on its platform are salvage-title vehicles, every lot is advertised and sold 'as is', and Copart is not a new- or used-car dealership; it encourages buyers to preview cars at its locations or use a third-party inspection service.
copart-mostly-salvage-as-is.licence_note: Copart's own 'common misconceptions' page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

copart-clean-title-not-undamaged.fact: In Copart's title definitions a 'clean title' vehicle is one that is operable or can be made so with some repairs, so a clean title is not a promise that the car is undamaged; a 'rebuilt title' car was once issued a salvage title and was then repaired and put through the state's required process (most states require an inspection by an authorised professional) to get a new title.
copart-clean-title-not-undamaged.licence_note: Copart help centre page (copyrighted, updated 2024-11-08): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

copart-vin-damage-codes.fact: Copart's list of damage codes includes VI (missing or altered VIN), VP (replaced VIN), FD (frame damage reported), RO (rollover), PR (partial or incomplete repair) and RJ (rejected repair), alongside everyday ones such as FR (front end), RR (rear end), HL (hail) and WA (water/flood).
copart-vin-damage-codes.licence_note: Copart help centre page (copyrighted, updated 2024-11-11): only the facts (the code list) are used, restated in our own words.

copart-enhanced-not-modified.fact: At Copart 'Enhanced Vehicle' does not mean a modified car: it means the seller requested, or Copart may use, enhancement services such as a wash, vacuum or protective covering, and the label does not guarantee that any service was actually done.
copart-enhanced-not-modified.licence_note: Copart's own terminology page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

odometer-original-tyres-20000.fact: NHTSA's tips against odometer fraud: examine the tyres; a car whose odometer shows 20,000 miles (about 32,000 km) or less should still have its original tyres. NHTSA also advises checking that wear on the accelerator, brake and clutch pedals fits the displayed mileage.
odometer-original-tyres-20000.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). nhtsa.gov blocks automated fetching, so the page was opened in a browser on 2026-10-12; restated in our own words. The km figure is our conversion (1 mile = 1.609344 km).

odometer-germany-every-third.fact: ADAC (page dated 27 January 2026): based on a large 2011 raid, German police estimate that the odometer has been tampered with on every third used car sold in Germany, raising its value by 3,000 euros per car on average; the estimated total damage in Germany is about 6 billion euros a year.
odometer-germany-every-third.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; the figure is the German police estimate as ADAC reports it, said as Germany's.

odometer-fault-memory-mileage.fact: ADAC: a cleanly done odometer manipulation cannot be detected by workshops or most car experts, and most OBD dongles cannot spot it either. One check is to have a workshop read the fault and service-interval memories: the mileages logged with some stored fault entries must not be higher than the total mileage shown on the instrument cluster.
odometer-fault-memory-mileage.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 27 January 2026): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as ADAC's advice.

odometer-oil-sticker-math.fact: ADAC: check the car's history for plausibility (repair invoices, inspection reports, fuel receipts, the service book and oil-change stickers or tags). An oil change is due after 40,000 km at the latest, so if a car supposedly has 100,000 km but its next oil change is marked for 180,000 km, something is wrong.
odometer-oil-sticker-math.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 27 January 2026): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; the example and the 40,000 km figure are ADAC's. NHTSA gives the same sticker advice: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/odometer-fraud.

short-trips-vs-long-miles.fact: ADAC: look not only at the mileage but at how the car was kept and used by its previous owners; a car with few kilometres built up on wear-heavy short trips can be more worn than one with many kilometres driven gently on long journeys.
short-trips-vs-long-miles.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 27 January 2026): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

odometer-km-filter.fact: ADAC: when a car cannot be manipulated electronically, fraudsters increasingly fit so-called mileage filters, which make the car count only a third to a half of the kilometres driven; unlike direct electronic manipulation, a workshop or Germany's periodic inspection (HU) can find such a filter, at least while it is still installed.
odometer-km-filter.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 27 January 2026): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

odometer-cluster-date.fact: ADAC: if odometer tampering is suspected, a workshop can find the production date of the instrument cluster and control units, usually stamped on the housing or on a sticker, because parts damaged during manipulation are sometimes replaced; a cluster made in 2021 does not fit a car built in 2019 unless the previous owner can document a replacement after a defect.
odometer-cluster-date.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 27 January 2026): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; the 2019/2021 example is ADAC's.

odometer-fraud-timing-belt.fact: ADAC: private buyers of a car with a faked mileage can be hit twice: besides the inflated price, they may think the timing-belt change still has time according to the displayed mileage, and if the belt snaps because its interval was unknowingly exceeded, the result can be engine damage costing thousands of euros in the worst case.
odometer-fraud-timing-belt.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 27 January 2026): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

contract-actual-mileage.fact: ADAC's lawyers advise not to rely on seller statements such as 'mileage as shown' or 'mileage read off', which are largely non-binding, and to insist that the purchase contract states the car's actual total mileage (in German law, a false written figure then means a promised quality is missing and entitles the buyer to withdraw).
contract-actual-mileage.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 25 March 2026): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; the legal effect is German law and is never said as Georgian law. The 'mileage as shown' wording is also on https://www.adac.de/rund-ums-fahrzeug/auto-kaufen-verkaufen/gebrauchtwagenkauf/tacho-manipulation/.

part-date-codes-age.fact: ADAC: most parts of a car carry a production date, usually only days or weeks before the whole car was built, often in coded form (for example an arrow in a circle of month numbers pointing at the month, plus the year's last two digits); seat belts and windows can carry one too. If the papers say first registration 2009 but a seat belt says 2005, either the car stood for a very long time before registration or the papers were tampered with.
part-date-codes-age.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 23 October 2024): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; the 2009/2005 example is ADAC's.

part-dates-reveal-repair.fact: ADAC: clear differences between the production dates of a car's parts can point to accident damage repaired with newer spare parts, which matters when the car is sold as accident-free.
part-dates-reveal-repair.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 23 October 2024): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

spare-wheel-dot-date.fact: ADAC: the DOT code on a tyre's sidewall gives the production week (first two digits) and year (last two); check the spare wheel too, whose DOT date should be from a similar period as the other wheels. Alloy wheels usually carry a cast production month and year on the inside, and steel wheels often a stamped date on the outer rim edge.
spare-wheel-dot-date.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 23 October 2024): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

tyre-three-digit-dot.fact: ADAC: a tyre whose DOT date code has only three digits instead of four was made under a format used only until the end of the 1990s, so it is extremely old and no longer usable.
tyre-three-digit-dot.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 23 October 2024): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

vin-model-year-not-build-year.fact: ADAC: most big makers code the model year in the 10th character of the VIN, but the model year is not necessarily the build year: depending on the maker it can begin as early as May or only in August of the previous year, so a car built at the end of 2017 can already be a 2018 model year.
vin-model-year-not-build-year.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 23 October 2024): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied. A different angle from vin-model-year (how to read the 10th character): this one is that model year is not build year.

vin-locations-match-papers.fact: ADAC: the VIN is in the registration papers, on many cars at the base of the windscreen where it can be read from outside, usually stamped into the body in the engine bay (for example on the bulkhead) and often near the seat mounting, and on stickers on the B-pillar visible when the driver's door is open. It must match the papers; a mismatch can mean a stolen car with false papers.
vin-locations-match-papers.licence_note: ADAC e.V. pages (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied. The locations are from the page above; the warning that a VIN mismatch can mean a stolen car with false papers is from https://www.adac.de/rund-ums-fahrzeug/auto-kaufen-verkaufen/gebrauchtwagenkauf/gebrauchtwagen-kaufen/ (dated 25 March 2026). GOV.UK gives the same advice (VIN and engine number must match the log book): https://www.gov.uk/checks-when-buying-a-used-car.

scam-escrow-prepayment.fact: ADAC: a common online scam offers a high-value car, usually located in another EU country, at a bargain price and asks the buyer to pay a supposedly safe escrow or transport company through a professional-looking fake website that soon disappears with the money. ADAC advises never paying in advance and letting money change hands only in person, in exchange for the car and its registration papers.
scam-escrow-prepayment.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 29 January 2026): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

scam-vin-clone-papers.fact: ADAC advises sellers never to copy or scan their car papers or ID and email them to would-be buyers: fraudsters abroad can grind the original VIN off a stolen car and stamp in the copied one, giving the stolen car a new identity (a so-called doublette, a cloned car).
scam-vin-clone-papers.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 29 January 2026): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

meet-at-registration-office.fact: ADAC describes buyers who meet a convincing seller, receive the papers, service book, inspection report and original keys with a matching VIN, and only at re-registration learn that the car is reported stolen and the papers are forged; to protect themselves, ADAC advises buyer and seller to meet directly at the registration office and re-register the car together.
meet-at-registration-office.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 29 January 2026): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as ADAC's advice (in Georgia the equivalent is the MIA Service Agency, whose procedures are not claimed here).

seller-pressure-red-flag.fact: ADAC: be careful if the seller pressures you to decide fast ('you must decide quickly', 'deregistering it today') or answers concrete questions with stock phrases ('they are all like that'); such time pressure can point to forged documents, and an offer that seems too good to be true may be a fraud.
seller-pressure-red-flag.licence_note: ADAC e.V. page (copyrighted, dated 25 March 2026): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

magnet-finds-filler.fact: RAC used-car checklist: ripples in the bodywork can mean a poor repair with filler, and a magnet can reveal it because filler is not magnetic (a magnet holds on a steel panel but not on body filler; aluminium and plastic parts never hold a magnet, so the test only works on steel panels).
magnet-finds-filler.licence_note: RAC page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's tip.

inspect-daylight-dry.fact: RAC: inspect a used car in clear daylight, because rain or darkness can hide a lot. ADAC gives the same advice: look at the car all round in brightness and good weather, otherwise rust spots, dents or scratches are easily missed.
inspect-daylight-dry.licence_note: RAC page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied. ADAC's matching advice: https://www.adac.de/rund-ums-fahrzeug/auto-kaufen-verkaufen/gebrauchtwagenkauf/gebrauchtwagen-kaufen/.

cold-start-not-warmed.fact: RAC: ask whether the seller has warmed the car up before you arrived, and if so, why; check that it starts from cold, then switch it off and restart it once warm, and check that it reaches operating temperature within 10 minutes and stays there.
cold-start-not-warmed.licence_note: RAC page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; the 10 minutes is the RAC's figure.

clutch-slip-hill-test.fact: RAC: on the test drive, try accelerating up a hill at low revs in a high gear to check whether the clutch slips; also notice how far up the pedal the clutch bites, and a quick getaway should not judder.
clutch-slip-hill-test.licence_note: RAC page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

view-at-seller-home.fact: RAC: view a privately sold car at the seller's home, so you can see that the address matches the registration document, and don't buy a car from a private seller in a public place.
view-at-seller-home.licence_note: RAC page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as the RAC's (UK) advice.

used-tyres-under-3mm.fact: RAC: the UK legal minimum tread depth is 1.6 mm, and if a used car's tyres have less than 3 mm, factor in the cost of changing them, because they will reach the legal limit very soon.
used-tyres-under-3mm.licence_note: RAC page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; 1.6 mm is UK law, said as the UK's.

rust-paint-bubbles.fact: RAC rust guide: exterior paint bubbling is often an early sign of rust, because oxidation commonly forms inside a panel and works its way outward. Check the frame rails under the doors, the wheel arches and the doors inside and out, and pull up the boot carpet: dampness or water damage on the carpet, in the footwells or the boot is usually a sign that the metal underneath has rusted.
rust-paint-bubbles.licence_note: RAC page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

airbag-light-must-flash.fact: Consumer Reports, warning signs of a rebuilt wreck: a dashboard airbag indicator that does not light up may mean the airbag was replaced improperly or not at all. With the ignition on, the warning lights should come on for a few seconds and then go out.
airbag-light-must-flash.licence_note: Consumer Reports page (copyrighted, 2012): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied. The 'lights come on for a few seconds, then go off' check is from Consumer Reports' used-car checklist, https://www.consumerreports.org/cars/how-to-inspect-a-used-car-a1377126659/.

frayed-belts-frontal-impact.fact: Consumer Reports: frayed seat belts or belt fibres melted together by friction point to a prior frontal impact at more than 15 mph (about 24 km/h).
frayed-belts-frontal-impact.licence_note: Consumer Reports page (copyrighted, 2012): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied. The km/h figure is our conversion.

fresh-undercoating-hides.fact: Consumer Reports: fresh undercoating on the wheel wells, chassis or engine strongly suggests hidden structural repairs that have been covered up.
fresh-undercoating-hides.licence_note: Consumer Reports page (copyrighted, 2012): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied. The used-car checklist repeats it: https://www.consumerreports.org/cars/how-to-inspect-a-used-car-a1377126659/.

overspray-on-seals.fact: Consumer Reports: paint overspray on chrome, trim or rubber seals points to a repaired neighbouring panel, and paint that chips off or does not match suggests a repair with poor colour blending.
overspray-on-seals.licence_note: Consumer Reports page (copyrighted, 2012): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

strut-tower-gouged-nuts.fact: Consumer Reports: damaged or gouged nuts and metal on the strut tower (the top suspension mount under the bonnet) may mean the frame was realigned.
strut-tower-gouged-nuts.licence_note: Consumer Reports page (copyrighted, 2012): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

capa-sticker-missing-badge.fact: Consumer Reports: a CAPA (Certified Automotive Parts Association) sticker on any part may indicate collision repair, and a missing emblem or model name on the boot lid may mean a non-original part was fitted.
capa-sticker-missing-badge.licence_note: Consumer Reports page (copyrighted, 2012): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as a sign on US cars.

bounce-test-shocks.fact: Consumer Reports: push down on each corner of the car; it should rebound once and then settle, and continued bouncing points to worn shock absorbers.
bounce-test-shocks.licence_note: Consumer Reports page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

tailpipe-residue-oil.fact: Consumer Reports: look at the residue in the tailpipe; black, greasy residue suggests burnt oil, while normal residue is dry and dark grey.
tailpipe-residue-oil.licence_note: Consumer Reports page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

clear-drips-ac-normal.fact: Consumer Reports: when checking under a car, clear drips on a hot day are usually just condensation from the air conditioning, while oil drips or green or red fluid beneath the engine are bad signs.
clear-drips-ac-normal.licence_note: Consumer Reports page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

auto-trans-fluid-colour.fact: Consumer Reports: check automatic transmission fluid with the engine warm and running; it should be pinkish, not brown, and smell like oil with no burnt odour, and metal particles on the rag are a serious warning.
auto-trans-fluid-colour.licence_note: Consumer Reports page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied. (Many modern automatics have no dipstick; the line says 'if it has one'.)

mileage-per-year-check.fact: Consumer Reports: divide the total mileage by the car's age; if it averages more than 20,000 miles (about 32,000 km) a year or fewer than 5,000 (about 8,000 km), ask why. A car with low miles should not show much wear on the pedal rubber.
mileage-per-year-check.licence_note: Consumer Reports page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; the km figures are our conversion.

doors-bonnet-close-square.fact: Consumer Reports: a door that does not close correctly could indicate a deformed door frame and a poor repair, and a bonnet or boot lid that does not close squarely may show twisting from a side impact.
doors-bonnet-close-square.licence_note: Consumer Reports page (copyrighted, 2012): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

flood-seatbelt-screws.fact: Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I): to spot a flood-damaged car, pull each seat belt all the way out and check the belt and retractor for moisture, mildew or grime, look for rust on screws in the console, and check the upholstery and door panels for fading.
flood-seatbelt-screws.licence_note: Insurance Information Institute page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied. A new angle beside flood-car-signs (FTC), which does not mention belts or screws.

uk-total-loss-actual-constructive.fact: UK government consumer guide to buying repaired written-off vehicles: an insurance total loss is either an actual loss (category A or B), a vehicle that cannot or should not be repaired and that DVLA will not re-register, or a constructive loss (category S or N), which could be repaired but would cost more to repair than its replacement value. Vehicles deemed an actual loss should never be repaired and returned to the road: even if they look repaired, their structural damage makes them unsafe.
uk-total-loss-actual-constructive.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words; said as the UK's categories.

mot-rust-30cm-rule.fact: UK MOT inspection manual: rust is judged by where it is. Load-bearing structure within 30 cm of the mounting points of the brakes, steering, suspension and other tested items is a 'prescribed area', and corrosion there fails the test if it has made a hole in the metal or the area does not feel firm under finger-and-thumb pressure.
mot-rust-30cm-rule.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words; said as the UK MOT's rule, never as Georgian law.

mot-filler-not-repair.fact: UK MOT inspection manual: repairs to load-bearing members must be properly done and appear as strong as the original structure; gas brazing, soldering, adhesive bonding, fibre reinforcement and body filler are not acceptable there, and patch repairs must normally be continuously seam-welded (spot welding only where the original panel was spot-welded and has been removed).
mot-filler-not-repair.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words; said as the UK MOT's rule.

euroncap-rating-six-years.fact: Euro NCAP: a car's star rating is valid for up to six years from the date it is awarded; after that it expires, not because the car changed but because safety standards evolved. Comparing ratings from different years is only meaningful if the rating system changed little in between, so the latest rating is always the most relevant.
euroncap-rating-six-years.licence_note: Euro NCAP page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied. The 2012/2024 pair in the line is our illustration, not Euro NCAP's.

depreciation-first-years.fact: Kelley Blue Book (US): most vehicles lose about 20% or more of their original value in the first year and about 30% over the first two years, then keep depreciating roughly 8-12% a year; mileage, age, reliability, number of owners and service history all affect it.
depreciation-first-years.licence_note: Kelley Blue Book page (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; said as KBB's US estimate.

obd-readiness-not-ready.fact: New York State DMV: a car's OBD 'readiness monitors' are self-tests of its emission systems (such as the catalytic converter or oxygen sensor), and they can show 'not ready' after recent repairs in which trouble codes were cleared with a scan tool, after the battery was recently disconnected or replaced, when the car's computer needs a software update, or when a pending problem has not yet turned on the check-engine light. Driving completes them; in most cases two drive cycles, separated by a cool-down period, are needed.
obd-readiness-not-ready.licence_note: New York State DMV page (state government): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

obd-permanent-codes.fact: California Bureau of Automotive Repair: permanent diagnostic trouble codes (PDTCs) cannot be erased by clearing codes with a scan tool or by disconnecting the battery; only the car's own OBD II system clears them, once it has verified that the fault is no longer present. Since 1 July 2019 California's Smog Check fails 2010 and newer vehicles with a PDTC present (some 2010 vehicles do not support PDTCs).
obd-permanent-codes.licence_note: California Bureau of Automotive Repair page (state government): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; the Smog Check rule is California's.

paint-layers-tenth-mm.fact: Ford paint research (2016 presentation hosted by NIST): factory body paint is a stack of thin layers, about 5 µm phosphate, 20 µm electrocoat, 25 µm primer, 10-20 µm basecoat (colour) and 45 µm clearcoat, roughly a tenth of a millimetre in total; a repaint adds basecoat and clearcoat, or primer, basecoat and clearcoat, on top.
paint-layers-tenth-mm.licence_note: Presentation by Mark Nichols, Ford Research and Advanced Engineering, 20 July 2016, hosted on nist.gov; Ford's work, not a US government work, so only the facts are used, restated in our own words. The 'about 0.1 mm' total is our sum of Ford's layer figures.

factory-repaint-5-10.fact: Ford paint research (2016): even in good factory paint shops only 90-95% of bodies come out right the first time; 5-10% of vehicles are repainted in the factory (basecoat and clearcoat, or primer, basecoat and clearcoat) and a small fraction twice, so extra paint layers can come from the factory too.
factory-repaint-5-10.licence_note: Presentation by Mark Nichols, Ford Research and Advanced Engineering, 20 July 2016, hosted on nist.gov; Ford's work, not a US government work, so only the facts are used, restated in our own words. Figures are Ford's.

windscreen-camera-calibration.fact: ADAC market survey (12 February 2026, 21 models): on modern cars, replacing the windscreen means removing the camera for automatic high beam and lane keeping and recalibrating it afterwards, so the job now costs a four-figure sum in euros in almost every case.
windscreen-camera-calibration.licence_note: ADAC e.V. press release (copyrighted): only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied; the cost range is ADAC's German survey, said as such.

ge-excise-age-cliff.fact: Georgian Tax Code, article 188 parts 12 and 13 as amended by law N1477 of 1 April 2026 (in force from 2 April 2026): the excise on a passenger car (HS heading 8703) is 1.50 GEL per cm³ of engine capacity for a car aged 0 to 6 years inclusive, and 4.50 GEL per cm³ for a car older than 6 years, three times as much.
ge-excise-age-cliff.licence_note: Law of Georgia N1477 amending the Tax Code, on matsne.gov.ge (official legal texts are not copyright-protected); restated in our own words. Said as Georgian law from 2 April 2026; transitional rules (art. 2) keep the old rates for cars shipped before that date. Rates can change, so re-check before reuse.

ge-excise-age-calendar-year.fact: Georgian Tax Code, article 188 part 18 (from 2 April 2026): for excise purposes an imported car's age is the difference between the year its customs declaration is registered and its year of manufacture, so only calendar years count: a 2020 car declared in December 2026 is 6, and declared in January 2027 it is 7, which moves it to the higher rate.
ge-excise-age-calendar-year.licence_note: Law of Georgia N1477 amending the Tax Code, on matsne.gov.ge (official legal texts are not copyright-protected); restated in our own words. The 2020/2026/2027 example is our worked example of the rule.

ge-excise-rhd-triple.fact: Georgian Tax Code, article 188 parts 15 to 17 (from 2 April 2026): a passenger car whose steering wheel is on the right, or has been moved, pays three times the excise rate of its age group, and a right-hand-drive electric car pays a flat 3,000 GEL.
ge-excise-rhd-triple.licence_note: Law of Georgia N1477 amending the Tax Code, on matsne.gov.ge (official legal texts are not copyright-protected); restated in our own words. Related bank facts: ge-steering-conversion-fails, rhd-headlights-dazzle.

ge-excise-hybrid-60.fact: Georgian Tax Code, article 188 part 14 (from 2 April 2026): for a left-hand-drive hybrid passenger car aged 0 to 6 years, the excise rate of 1.50 GEL per cm³ is reduced by 60%; the law writes this reduction only for that age group.
ge-excise-hybrid-60.licence_note: Law of Georgia N1477 amending the Tax Code, on matsne.gov.ge (official legal texts are not copyright-protected); restated in our own words.

ge-import-register-60-days.fact: Georgia's MIA Service Agency: a motor vehicle brought into Georgia from abroad for registration must be registered within 60 days.
ge-import-register-60-days.licence_note: Ministry of Internal Affairs Service Agency of Georgia, official page: only the facts are used, restated in our own words.

ge-remote-transfer.fact: Georgia's MIA Service Agency announced on 24 July 2026 a new service for re-registering (transferring) a vehicle remotely, which citizens can use through the agency's SERVICE AGENCY mobile app and its website sa.gov.ge.
ge-remote-transfer.licence_note: Ministry of Internal Affairs Service Agency of Georgia, official news page: only the facts are used, restated in our own words. The page gives no procedure details, so the film may not invent steps.

hc-breakdown-triangle-45m.fact: UK Highway Code rule 276: after a breakdown, get the vehicle off the road if possible and use hazard lights if it is causing an obstruction. Place a warning triangle at least 45 metres (147 feet) behind it on the same side of the road (the UK Code says never on motorways; Georgian law, Article 52, requires one, at least 15 m behind in a settlement and 30 m outside). Wear light or fluorescent clothing by day and reflective clothing at night, and do not stand between your vehicle and oncoming traffic.
hc-breakdown-triangle-45m.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-motorway-breakdown-get-out.fact: UK Highway Code rule 277: if you break down on a motorway, try to reach an emergency area or hard shoulder and stop as far left as possible with the wheels turned to the left (the UK drives on the left). Leave the vehicle by the side furthest from traffic if it is safe and possible to do so, and do not return to it even if it is raining, cold or dark. The UK Code also says not to place a warning triangle on the carriageway (Georgian law, Article 52, does require one). If you cannot reach a place of relative safety or leave the vehicle safely, stay inside with seat belts and hazard lights on and call 999.
hc-motorway-breakdown-get-out.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-crash-scene-engines-off.fact: UK Highway Code rule 283: at a collision, use hazard lights, ask drivers to switch off their engines and stop smoking, and call the emergency services with the exact location and the casualties. Move uninjured people to safety. Do not move injured people from their vehicles unless they are in immediate danger, and do not remove a motorcyclist's helmet unless it is essential and you are trained to do so.
hc-crash-scene-engines-off.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-motorway-dropped-object.fact: UK Highway Code rule 280: if anything falls from a vehicle onto a motorway or other high-speed road, do not try to remove it yourself. Stop in a place of relative safety and call 999. On other roads, remove an obstruction only if it is safe to do so.
hc-motorway-dropped-object.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-dangerous-goods-orange-plates.fact: UK Highway Code rules 284 and 285: vehicles carrying dangerous goods in packages show plain orange reflective plates, and road tankers show hazard warning plates. At an incident involving such a vehicle, switch off engines and do not smoke, keep well away, and do not try to rescue casualties, because you could become one yourself. Give the emergency services as much detail from the plates as you can, and do not use a mobile phone close to a vehicle carrying flammable loads.
hc-dangerous-goods-orange-plates.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-hazard-lights-not-parking.fact: UK Highway Code rule 116: hazard warning lights may be used while the vehicle is stationary, to warn that it is temporarily blocking traffic. They are never an excuse for dangerous or illegal parking. They must not be used while driving or being towed, except on a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway to warn drivers behind of a hazard or obstruction ahead.
hc-hazard-lights-not-parking.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-pets-restrained.fact: UK Highway Code rule 57: in a vehicle, dogs and other animals should be suitably restrained so they cannot distract you while you drive or injure you, or themselves, if you stop quickly. A seat belt harness, pet carrier, dog cage or dog guard are ways to restrain them.
hc-pets-restrained.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

hc-first-aid-burns-kit.fact: UK Highway Code Annex 7 (first aid on the road): cool a burn for at least 20 minutes with plenty of clean, cool water. Always carry a first aid kit: you may never need it, but it could save a life.
hc-first-aid-burns-kit.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

ge-crash-driver-duties.fact: Georgian traffic law (Article 27): a driver involved in a road accident must stop at once without moving the vehicle and switch on the hazard lights, then make sure nobody was injured or killed. They must report the accident immediately to the relevant Interior Ministry service and stay at the scene until an authorised officer arrives, unless an injured person urgently needs taking to hospital. They must not change the scene or destroy evidence, must write down witnesses' surnames, and must arrange first aid and call emergency medical help.
ge-crash-driver-duties.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-crash-no-injury-sketch.fact: Georgian traffic law (Article 27): if nobody was injured in the accident, the drivers may agree, draw up a sketch of the incident themselves, sign it and go to the nearest patrol police unit to have it registered.
ge-crash-no-injury-sketch.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-railway-crossing-stall.fact: Georgian traffic law (Article 39): if a vehicle is forced to stop on a railway crossing, the driver must try to get it off the tracks. If that is impossible, they must warn the train driver in time and get the passengers out at once. Where possible, they send two people along the tracks, one each way, up to 1,000 metres from the crossing, to signal the approaching train to stop. The stop signal is a circular movement of the arm, using a brightly coloured cloth or object by day and a torch or lantern at night.
ge-railway-crossing-stall.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

oli-stalled-tracks-45-degrees.fact: Operation Lifesaver (US rail safety nonprofit, North Carolina page): if your vehicle stalls on the tracks and a train is approaching, move away from the tracks toward the train at a 45-degree angle, because moving in the train's direction of travel can get you hit by flying debris. A freight train at 55 mph (about 89 km/h) can take a mile (about 1.6 km) or more to stop once the emergency brakes are applied. (The page also says to get out even if no train is visible; Georgian law, Article 39, instead requires first trying to clear the tracks, so that part is not used.)
oli-stalled-tracks-45-degrees.licence_note: Operation Lifesaver, Inc. page (copyright Operation Lifesaver). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

ge-112-app-location.fact: Georgia's 112 emergency service app can place a call to 112 and send the caller's location coordinates at the same time. Its chat sends the coordinates by SMS if the phone has no mobile data. Its SOS button is a silent alarm for when making a call could create or increase danger: it sends the user's location and 112 dispatches police there. Each feature needs the phone's GPS switched on.
ge-112-app-location.licence_note: Page of LEPL 112, Georgia's public emergency service. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

eu-ecall-sos-button.fact: EU: new car models approved for manufacture after 31 March 2018 (cars with up to 8 seats and light commercial vehicles) must have 112-based eCall. After a serious accident it automatically makes a free 112 call, and it can also be set off by pressing a button. It sends the exact location, the time of the accident, the vehicle identification number and the direction of travel. The rest of the time it stays inactive, with no tracking. Cars registered earlier need not be retrofitted.
eu-ecall-sos-button.licence_note: Your Europe (europa.eu), copyright European Union; reuse authorised with acknowledgement of the source (Commission Decision 2011/833/EU). Restated in our own words.

adac-warning-triangle-carry.fact: ADAC (German auto club): put on a high-visibility vest and switch on the hazard lights. Then walk along the outer edge of the road, or better behind the crash barrier facing the traffic, carrying the opened warning triangle in front of you at about chest height so oncoming drivers see you better. Under German guidance, place it about 50 m back in town, about 100 m on country roads and at least 150 m on the motorway. If a bend or a crest lies within that distance, the triangle always goes before it.
adac-warning-triangle-carry.licence_note: ADAC page (copyright ADAC e.V.). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

adac-crash-photos-evidence.fact: ADAC (German auto club): after securing the scene and giving first aid, collect evidence. Photograph the accident scene and the damage to the cars, look for witnesses and note their details, and exchange details with the other driver.
adac-crash-photos-evidence.licence_note: ADAC page (copyright ADAC e.V.). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

uk-child-seat-135cm.fact: UK rules: children must normally use a child car seat until they are 12 years old or 135 cm tall, whichever comes first. Height-based seats approved under R129 must face backwards until the child is over 15 months old. Front airbags must be deactivated before a rear-facing baby seat is fitted in a front seat.
uk-child-seat-135cm.licence_note: GOV.UK, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

cdc-rear-facing-2-to-4.fact: CDC (US): children should ride in a rear-facing car seat from birth until about age 2 to 4, or until they reach the seat's maximum height or weight limit, kept rear-facing as long as possible. After that they use a forward-facing seat with a harness and top tether until at least age 5, and they ride in the back seat until age 13.
cdc-rear-facing-2-to-4.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

cdc-top-tether.fact: CDC (US): use the top tether with forward-facing car seats. A top tether can reduce a child's head movement in a crash by about 4 to 6 inches (about 10 to 15 cm).
cdc-top-tether.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

cdc-belt-fit-booster.fact: CDC (US): a child moves from a booster seat to the seat belt alone only when the belt fits properly, usually at age 9 to 12. The lap belt should lie across the upper thighs, not the stomach, and the shoulder belt should cross the middle of the shoulder and the chest, not the neck or face.
cdc-belt-fit-booster.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

aap-bulky-coat-harness.fact: American Academy of Pediatrics: bulky clothing such as winter coats and snowsuits should not be worn under a car seat harness. In a crash the fluffy padding flattens at once and leaves extra space under the harness, through which a child can slip. If you can pinch the harness strap, it needs tightening.
aap-bulky-coat-harness.licence_note: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (copyright AAP). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

rospa-child-seat-after-crash.fact: RoSPA (UK): a child car seat that has been in a crash should be replaced even if no damage is visible, because it may be weakened and will not protect as well in another crash. It may not need replacing only if the impact was at very low speed, the car had little or no external damage and no child was in the seat. If in doubt, replace it.
rospa-child-seat-after-crash.licence_note: RoSPA child car seats site (copyright Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

rospa-second-hand-child-seat.fact: RoSPA (UK): the best advice is not to buy a second-hand child car seat, because you cannot be certain of its history. It may have been in a crash with damage that is not visible, its instructions are often missing, and it may be old and not built to current standards. Use one only from family or friends, and only if you are absolutely sure of its history, it has its original instructions and it is not too old.
rospa-second-hand-child-seat.licence_note: RoSPA child car seats site (copyright Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

udv-child-seat-misuse.fact: German Insurers Accident Research (UDV, part of the German Insurance Association) field study of 1,042 children: 52.4 percent were secured correctly and 47.6 percent incorrectly. Misuse was very significantly lower with ISOFIX seats than with child seats held by the three-point seat belt.
udv-child-seat-misuse.licence_note: UDV (German Insurers Accident Research) page, copyright GDV. Only the figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

rospa-seatbelt-replace-after-crash.fact: RoSPA (UK): in a crash the webbing of a seat belt stretches and absorbs some of the energy. A belt that has restrained someone in a crash is more likely to cause injury in another one and must always be replaced. Fraying at the edges, cuts, holes or a damaged buckle also make a belt less effective.
rospa-seatbelt-replace-after-crash.licence_note: RoSPA road safety factsheet 'Seatbelts: Advice and Information' (October 2018), copyright RoSPA. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

rospa-pregnant-seatbelt.fact: RoSPA (UK): the safest way for a pregnant woman to wear a seat belt is the diagonal strap between the breasts and over the shoulder, not the neck, and the lap belt flat on the thighs, beneath the bump and over the pelvis, not the bump, worn as tight as possible. Pregnant women should not wear lap-only belts.
rospa-pregnant-seatbelt.licence_note: RoSPA road safety factsheet 'Seatbelts: Advice and Information' (October 2018), copyright RoSPA. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

iihs-unbelted-rear-kills-driver.fact: IIHS (citing Bose et al., 2013): in frontal crashes, an unbelted rear-seat passenger sitting behind a belted driver increases the driver's risk of death by 137% compared with a belted rear passenger. IIHS also cites MacLennan et al. (2004): exposure to unbelted occupants increases the risk of injury or death to other occupants in the vehicle by 40%.
iihs-unbelted-rear-kills-driver.licence_note: IIHS topic page (copyright Insurance Institute for Highway Safety). Only the figures are used, restated in our own words with the studies IIHS cites, no text copied.

iihs-ejection-risk.fact: IIHS (citing NHTSA, 2010): occupants ejected from the vehicle in non-rollover crashes are nearly twice as likely to die, and those ejected in rollover crashes are 4 times as likely to die.
iihs-ejection-risk.licence_note: IIHS topic page (copyright Insurance Institute for Highway Safety). Only the figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

race-loose-objects.fact: RACE (Spanish royal auto club): in a crash at just 50 km/h, loose objects in the cabin can weigh up to 30 to 40 times their own mass. A 4 kg bag hits with a force of about 160 kg, a 950 g umbrella about 38 kg, and an unsecured child seat of about 20 kg about 800 kg. All objects and luggage should go in the boot, or else in the cabin's gloveboxes and storage compartments, such as the pockets behind the front seats.
race-loose-objects.licence_note: RACE (Real Automóvil Club de España) page, copyright RACE. Only the figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

icbc-head-restraint-height.fact: ICBC (British Columbia's public auto insurer): set the top of the head restraint at least level with the top of your head and as close to the back of your head as possible, adjusting the seat back if needed. Soft-tissue neck and back injuries (whiplash) are the most common crash injuries, and well-designed, properly adjusted head restraints can reduce injuries in rear-impact crashes by 24 to 44 percent.
icbc-head-restraint-height.licence_note: ICBC (Insurance Corporation of British Columbia) page, copyright ICBC. Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

tc-airbag-25cm.fact: Transport Canada: sitting 25 cm from the driver airbag, measured from the centre of the steering wheel to the centre of the breastbone, gives a clear margin of safety, because the risk zone of an airbag is the first 8 cm of its inflation. If you cannot get 25 cm, move the seat back as far as you can while still reaching the pedals, recline the seat back slightly, raise yourself with a firm cushion or the seat height adjuster, and tilt an adjustable wheel downward so the airbag points at your chest rather than your head and neck.
tc-airbag-25cm.licence_note: Transport Canada page; reuse terms are non-commercial: facts only, restated in our own words, no text copied.

nhtsa-airbag-not-every-crash.fact: NHTSA (US): frontal airbags are generally designed to deploy in moderate to severe frontal crashes. That means a crash equal to hitting a solid fixed barrier at 8 to 14 mph (about 13 to 23 km/h) or more, or a parked car of similar size at about 16 to 28 mph (about 26 to 45 km/h) or more. Airbags are not meant to deploy in every crash, because in a milder one the seat belt may protect enough.
nhtsa-airbag-not-every-crash.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

nhtsa-airbag-once-used-cars.fact: NHTSA (US): an airbag can deploy only once and must be replaced by an authorized service technician without delay, before the vehicle is driven again. In used vehicles, one possible reason an airbag does not deploy is that it was never replaced after a previous crash.
nhtsa-airbag-once-used-cars.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

nhtsa-fake-airbag-inflators.fact: NHTSA (US): fake airbags have been found in vehicles where an airbag was replaced, for example after a crash, and were sold online to consumers or repair shops. Counterfeit airbags have been shown to consistently malfunction, from not deploying at all to throwing out metal shrapnel. In 2024, NHTSA issued a consumer alert after cheap, faulty aftermarket replacement airbag inflators killed at least three people and left two with life-altering injuries. It urges used-car buyers to learn the vehicle's history and make sure its airbag inflators are genuine.
nhtsa-fake-airbag-inflators.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

nrma-feet-on-dash.fact: NRMA (Australian motoring club): in a 2017 test at the NSW roads agency's Crashlab, a Holden Commodore hit a wall at 70 km/h. The passenger airbag drove the dummy's feet, which rested on the dashboard, back into its face, and the dummy slid down under the belt so its internal organs took the impact. NRMA reports that more than 400 passengers were admitted to hospital in 2016 with injuries linked to feet on the dashboard.
nrma-feet-on-dash.licence_note: NRMA page (copyright NRMA). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

usfa-car-fire.fact: US Fire Administration: if your car catches fire, pull over as soon as it is safe, turn off the engine, get everyone out and never go back into the vehicle. Do not try to fight the fire yourself. Keep everyone at least 100 feet (about 30 m) from the burning vehicle and away from traffic. Do not open the hood or trunk if you think the fire is under it, because this could make the fire grow. Then call the emergency number.
usfa-car-fire.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

usfa-fuel-cans.fact: US Fire Administration: keep gas cans or propane tanks away from passengers, sealed tightly and standing upright on a flat surface so they stay upright. If you must carry them inside the vehicle, keep the windows open so fumes do not build up.
usfa-fuel-cans.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

cdc-co-attached-garage.fact: CDC (US): never run a car or truck inside a garage attached to a house, even with the garage door open. In a detached garage, always open the door to let in fresh air when a vehicle is running inside.
cdc-co-attached-garage.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

cdc-co-tailgate-open.fact: CDC (US): if only the tailgate of a car or SUV is open, carbon monoxide from the exhaust will be pulled into the vehicle.
cdc-co-tailgate-open.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

cdc-co-exhaust-leak.fact: CDC (US): a small leak in the exhaust system can let carbon monoxide build up inside the car, so have a mechanic check the exhaust system every year. CO symptoms are often described as flu-like: headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion. People who are sleeping or drunk can die of CO poisoning before they have symptoms.
cdc-co-exhaust-leak.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

nws-lightning-metal-shell.fact: US National Weather Service: a hard-topped metal vehicle with the windows closed protects the people inside from lightning because of its outer metal shell, not its rubber tyres. A strike typically travels through the metal shell and then through the tyres to the ground. It very often destroys one or more tyres, and it can damage the electronics or start a fire.
nws-lightning-metal-shell.licence_note: US federal government work (NOAA/NWS), public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

eca-earthquake-driving.fact: Earthquake Country Alliance (with SCEC, headquartered at the University of Southern California): if an earthquake starts while you are driving, pull over to the side of the road, stop and set the parking brake. Avoid overpasses, bridges, power lines, signs, trees and other hazards, and stay inside the vehicle until the shaking stops.
eca-earthquake-driving.licence_note: Earthquake Country Alliance page (copyright Statewide California Earthquake Center, USC). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

eca-power-line-on-car.fact: Earthquake Country Alliance: if a power line falls on your car, stay inside until a trained person removes the wire.
eca-power-line-on-car.licence_note: Earthquake Country Alliance page (copyright Statewide California Earthquake Center, USC). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

nws-half-tank-cold.fact: US National Weather Service: during extreme cold, keep at least half a tank of fuel in your vehicle so that you can stay warm if you become stranded.
nws-half-tank-cold.licence_note: US federal government work (NOAA/NWS), public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

nws-stranded-be-seen.fact: US National Weather Service (Sterling, Virginia office): if stranded in a winter storm, stay in the vehicle unless shelter is visible nearby, because people become disoriented quickly in wind-driven snow and cold. Make yourself visible: turn on the dome light at night, tie a coloured cloth, preferably red, to the antenna or door, and raise the hood once the snow stops. Move arms, legs, fingers and toes vigorously from time to time to keep the blood flowing.
nws-stranded-be-seen.licence_note: US federal government work (NOAA/NWS), public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

nws-winter-car-kit.fact: US National Weather Service winter car survival kit: jumper cables (flares or a reflective triangle are useful extras), flashlights with spare batteries, a first aid kit, water and non-perishable food, a basic toolkit, a battery or hand-crank radio, cat litter or sand for tyre traction, a shovel, an ice scraper, warm clothes, gloves, a hat and boots, blankets or sleeping bags, and a charged phone with a spare charger.
nws-winter-car-kit.licence_note: US federal government work (NOAA/NWS), public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

aap-child-heats-faster.fact: American Academy of Pediatrics: a child's body heats up 3 to 5 times faster than an adult's. A child's major organs begin to shut down at 104 °F (40 °C), and a child can die at 107 °F (about 41.7 °C). A car can heat up by 20 °F (about 11 °C) in 10 minutes, and heatstroke can happen at outside temperatures as low as 57 °F (about 14 °C). Cracking a window, parking in the shade or running the air conditioner does little to lower the temperature inside.
aap-child-heats-faster.licence_note: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (copyright AAP). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

aap-back-seat-reminder.fact: American Academy of Pediatrics: to avoid forgetting a child in the car, always check the back seat before locking the car and walking away, and put your phone, bag, backpack or purse in the back seat so you have to look there when you arrive. Ask your child care provider to call if your child is more than 10 minutes late. Keep the car locked when parked and the keys out of children's reach, so a curious child cannot get in.
aap-back-seat-reminder.licence_note: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (copyright AAP). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

noheatstroke-forgotten.fact: NoHeatStroke.org (Jan Null, Department of Meteorology and Climate Science, San Jose State University): of 1,041 US child hot-car deaths from 1998 to 2025, based on media reports, 52.9% were children forgotten by a caregiver, 23.8% got into the car on their own, 21.9% were knowingly left in the car, and 1.3% are unknown.
noheatstroke-forgotten.licence_note: NoHeatStroke.org (Jan Null, San Jose State University); reproduction only under its attribution policy, so only the figures are used, restated in our own words and credited to NoHeatStroke.org.

he-deer-dip-beam.fact: Highways England with The Deer Initiative (UK, October 2018): October to December is a high-risk period for deer collisions, and the greatest risk is from sunset to midnight and in the hours shortly before and after sunrise. Use full beam when you can, but dip it when you see deer, because they may freeze. More deer may follow the first one you see. Avoid sudden swerving, since hitting oncoming traffic or another obstacle could be even worse, and use hazard lights if you have to stop.
he-deer-dip-beam.licence_note: GOV.UK news release, Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0 (free reuse with attribution: 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0'). Restated in our own words.

bc-brake-dont-swerve.fact: Government of British Columbia: scan the ditches for movement or for eyes reflecting your headlights, using high beams when possible. Many animals travel in groups, so if you see one, slow down until you are well past. Be extra careful at dawn, dusk and night. Never swerve suddenly to avoid an animal, because this can lead to a more serious collision: brake firmly and stay in your lane.
bc-brake-dont-swerve.licence_note: Province of British Columbia page (copyright Province of British Columbia). Only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

ev-cold-range-41.fact: fueleconomy.gov (US DOE/EPA, based on a 2019 AAA study): at -7 °C (20 °F) an electric car's range in mixed city and highway driving can drop by about 41% (its efficiency by about 39%), and about two-thirds of the extra energy consumed goes into heating the cabin. With the cabin heater off, range is only about 12% lower at -7 °C (20 °F) than at 24 °C (75 °F).
ev-cold-range-41.licence_note: US federal government work (fueleconomy.gov, DOE/EPA), public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

ev-hybrid-heat-vs-cold.fact: AAA lab tests (May 2026; three EVs and three hybrids, cabin set to 22 °C/72 °F): at -7 °C (20 °F) EV range fell 39.0% and hybrid fuel economy 22.8%; at 35 °C (95 °F), compared with 24 °C (75 °F), EV range fell only 8.5% and hybrid fuel economy 12.0%.
ev-hybrid-heat-vs-cold.licence_note: AAA newsroom page, copyrighted: only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

ev-precondition-plugged-in.fact: AAA (May 2026), among its efficiency tips for EV and hybrid drivers: precondition (heat or cool) the cabin while the car is still plugged in, and use targeted comfort features such as seat and steering-wheel heating.
ev-precondition-plugged-in.licence_note: AAA newsroom page, copyrighted: only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

ev-fast-charge-stop-at-80.fact: ADAC: at a DC fast charger the charging power drops off sharply after about 80% state of charge, so the last 20% takes comparatively long. ADAC's rule of thumb for trips: plug in at roughly 10-30% and unplug at about 80%.
ev-fast-charge-stop-at-80.licence_note: ADAC (German automobile club) page, copyrighted: only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

ev-charger-power-car-decides.fact: ADAC: the power written on a fast charger is the most it can deliver, not a guaranteed minimum; a car that can only take 50 or 100 kW gains nothing from a 400 kW point, and stations with several points often split their power when several cars charge at once (for example one 150 kW point becomes two 75 kW points).
ev-charger-power-car-decides.licence_note: ADAC (German automobile club) page, copyrighted: only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

ev-cold-battery-slow-charge.fact: ADAC: a battery that has cooled down overnight in winter will not reach anywhere near maximum power at a fast charger (the ideal battery temperature is generally 20-40 °C). Most modern EVs can heat the battery first (preconditioning), but most do it automatically only when the navigation is guiding the car to a fast charger.
ev-cold-battery-slow-charge.licence_note: ADAC (German automobile club) page, copyrighted: only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

ev-daily-charge-80.fact: ADAC battery care: for everyday use charging an EV to 80% is usually enough and protects the battery; recharge at about 10-20% instead of running it down; charge to 100% only when needed, e.g. just before a long trip; for long parking such as holidays, leave it at about 30-70%.
ev-daily-charge-80.licence_note: ADAC (German automobile club) page, copyrighted: only the facts are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

ev-charging-speeds-ac-dc.fact: US Department of Energy (AFDC): a Level 2 AC charger (240 V; most home units deliver 7.2 kW) adds roughly 25 miles (about 40 km) of range per hour of charging, while DC fast charging adds roughly 100 to 200+ miles (about 160-320 km) per 30 minutes; charging power varies with the vehicle and its state of charge.
ev-charging-speeds-ac-dc.licence_note: US federal government work (afdc.energy.gov, DOE), public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

ev-77-percent-to-wheels.fact: fueleconomy.gov: electric cars turn over 77% of the electrical energy taken from the grid into power at the wheels, while conventional petrol cars turn only about 12-30% of the energy in petrol into power at the wheels.
ev-77-percent-to-wheels.licence_note: US federal government work (fueleconomy.gov, DOE/EPA), public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

ev-battery-lifespan-years.fact: fueleconomy.gov: an electric car's battery may last 12 to 15 years in moderate climates and 8 to 12 years in severe climates, and replacement batteries are expensive.
ev-battery-lifespan-years.licence_note: US federal government work (fueleconomy.gov, DOE/EPA), public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

eu-battery-durability-80-72.fact: Under the EU's Euro 7 rules (provisional deal December 2023, adopted as Regulation (EU) 2024/1257), batteries of new electric and plug-in hybrid cars must keep at least 80% of their starting capacity up to 5 years or 100,000 km, and at least 72% up to 8 years or 160,000 km.
